   - `pgCluster` - the name of your cluster. Check it with the `kubectl get pg -n $NAMESPACE` command
   - `method` - the backup method. Specify `volumeSnapshot`.

   Here’s the example configuration:

   ```
   apiVersion: pgv2.percona.com/v2
   kind: PerconaPGBackup
   metadata:
     name: my-snapshot-backup
   spec:
     pgCluster: cluster1
     method: volumeSnapshot
   ```

1. Apply the configuration to start a backup:

   ```
   kubectl apply -f deploy/backup.yaml -n $NAMESPACE
   ```

1. Check the backup status:

   ```
   kubectl get pg-backup my-snapshot-backup -n $NAMESPACE
   ```

   Sample output

   ```
   NAME      CLUSTER    REPO    DESTINATION   STATUS      TYPE   COMPLETED   AGE
   my-snapshot-backup                      cluster1   repo1                 Succeeded   snapshot   3m38s       3m53s
   ```

## Make a scheduled snapshot-based backup

1. Configure the backup schedule in your cluster Custom Resource. Edit the `deploy/cr.yaml` manifest. In the `schedule` key in the `volumeSnapshots` subsection under `backups`, specify the schedule in the Cron format for the snapshots to be made automatically. Your updated configuration should look like this:

   ```
   apiVersion: pgv2.percona.com/v2
   kind: PerconaPGCluster
   metadata:
     name: my-cluster
   spec:
     backups:
       volumeSnapshots:
         className: my-snapshot-class
         mode: offline
         schedule: "0 3 * * *"   # Every day at 3:00 AM
   ```

1. Apply the configuration to update the cluster:

   ```
   kubectl apply -f deploy/cr.yaml -n $NAMESPACE
   ```

## In-place restore from a PVC snapshot

An in-place restore is a restore to the same cluster using the `PerconaPGRestore` custom resource. You can make a full in-place restore or a point-in-time restore.

When you create the `PerconaPGRestore` object, the Operator performs the following steps:

1. Suspends all instances in the cluster.
1. Deletes all existing PVCs in the cluster. This removes all existing data, WAL, and tablespaces.
1. Creates new PVCs with the snapshot serving as the data source. This restores the data, WAL, and tablespaces from that snapshot.
1. Spins up a job to configure the restored PVCs to be used by the cluster.
1. Resumes all instances in the cluster. The cluster starts with the data from the snapshot.

Important

An in-place restore overwrites the current data and is destructive. Any data that was written after the backup was made is lost. Therefore, consider restoring to a new cluster instead. This way you can evaluate the data before switching to the new cluster and don’t risk losing data in the existing cluster.

Follow the steps below to make a full in-place restore from a PVC snapshot.

1. Configure the `PerconaPGRestore` object. Edit the `deploy/restore.yaml` manifest and specify the following keys:

   - `pgCluster` - the name of your cluster. Check it with the `kubectl get pg -n $NAMESPACE` command
   - `volumeSnapshotBackupName` - the name of the PVC snapshot backup. Check it with the `kubectl get pg-backup -n $NAMESPACE` command.

   Here’s the example configuration:

   ```
   apiVersion: pgv2.percona.com/v2
   kind: PerconaPGRestore
   metadata:
     name: restore1
   spec:
     pgCluster: cluster1
     volumeSnapshotBackupName: my-snapshot-backup
   ```

1. Apply the configuration to start a restore:

   ```
   kubectl apply -f deploy/restore.yaml -n $NAMESPACE
   ```

1. Check the restore status:

   ```
   kubectl get pg-restore restore1 -n $NAMESPACE
   ```

   Sample output

   ```
   NAME         CLUSTER      STATUS      COMPLETED              AGE
   restore1     cluster1     Succeeded   2026-02-16T11:00:00Z   2m20s
   ```

## In-place restore with point-in-time recovery

You can make a [point-in-time restore](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/backups-pitr.html) from a PVC snapshot and replay WAL files from a WAL archive made with pgBackRest. For this scenario, your cluster must meet the following requirements:

1. Have a `pgBackRest` configuration, including the backup storage and at least one repository. See the [Configure backup storage](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/backups-storage.html) section for configuration steps.
1. The repository must have at least one WAL archive.

The workflow for point-in-time restore is similar to [a full in-place restore](#in-place-restore-from-a-pvc-snapshot). After the Operator restores the data from the snapshot, it replays the WAL files from the WAL archive to bring the cluster to the target time.

Important

An in-place restore overwrites the current data and is destructive. Any data that was written after the backup was made is lost. Therefore, consider restoring to a new cluster instead. This way you can evaluate the data before switching to the new cluster and don’t risk losing data in the existing cluster.

Follow the steps below to make a point-in-time restore from a PVC snapshot.

1. Check the repo name and the target time for the restore.

   - List the backups:

   ```
   kubectl get pg-backup -n $NAMESPACE
   ```

   - For a `pgBackRest` backup run the following command to get the [latest restorable time](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/backups-pitr.html#latest-restorable-time):

   ```
   kubectl get pg-backup <backup_name> -n $NAMESPACE -o jsonpath='{.status.latestRestorableTime}'
   ```

1. Configure the `PerconaPGRestore` object. Edit the `deploy/restore.yaml` manifest and specify the following keys:

   - `pgCluster` - the name of your cluster. Check it with the `kubectl get pg -n $NAMESPACE` command

   - `volumeSnapshotBackupName` - the name of the PVC snapshot backup.

   - `repoName` - the name of the pgBackRest repository that contains the WAL archives.

   - `options` - the options for the restore. Specify the following options:

     - `--type=time` - set to `time` to make a point-in-time restore.
     - `--target` - set the target time for the restore.

   Here’s the example configuration:

   ```
   apiVersion: pgv2.percona.com/v2
   kind: PerconaPGRestore
   metadata:
     name: pitr-restore
   spec:
     pgCluster: cluster1
     volumeSnapshotBackupName: my-snapshot-backup
     repoName: repo1
     options:
       - --type=time
       - --target="2026-02-16T11:00:00Z"
   ```

1. Apply the configuration to start a restore:

   ```
   kubectl apply -f deploy/restore.yaml -n $NAMESPACE
   ```

1. Check the restore status:

   ```
   kubectl get pg-restore pitr-restore -n $NAMESPACE
   ```

## Create a new cluster from a PVC snapshot

You can create a new cluster from a PVC snapshot. This is useful when you want to restore the data to a new cluster and don’t want to overwrite the existing data in the existing cluster.

To create a new cluster from a PVC snapshot, you need to configure the `PerconaPGCluster` object and specify an `volumesnapshot` object as the `dataSource`. You also need to configure the `instances` and `backups` sections to set up the new cluster.

For more information about the `dataSource` options, see the [Choose a `dataSource` option](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/backups-clone.html#choose-a-datasource-option) section. Also check the [Custom Resource reference](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/operator.html#datasource-subsection) for all available options.

Follow the steps below to create a new cluster from a PVC snapshot.

1. Create the namespace where a new cluster will be deployed and export it as the environment variable:

   ```
   kubectl create namespace <new-namespace>
   export NEW_NAMESPACE=<new-namespace>
   ```

1. Configure the `PerconaPGCluster` object. Edit the `deploy/cr.yaml` manifest and specify the following keys:

   - `dataSource` - the name of the PVC snapshot backup. Check it with the `kubectl get pg-backup my-snapshot-backup -o jsonpath='{.status.snapshot.dataVolumeSnapshotRef}'` command on the **source** cluster.
   - `instances` - the instances configuration for the new cluster.
   - `backups` - the backups configuration for the new cluster.

   Here’s the example configuration:

   ```
   apiVersion: pgv2.percona.com/v2
   kind: PerconaPGCluster
   metadata:
     name: new-cluster
   spec:
     instances:
       - name: instance1
         replicas: 3
         dataVolumeClaimSpec:
           accessModes:
             - ReadWriteOnce
           resources:
             requests:
               storage: 10Gi
     dataSource:
       apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io
       kind: VolumeSnapshot
       name: <name-of-the-pvc-snapshot-backup>
   ```

1. Apply the configuration to create the new cluster:

   ```
   kubectl apply -f deploy/cr.yaml -n $NEW_NAMESPACE
   ```

The new cluster will be provisioned shortly using the volume of the source cluster.

# Configure backup encryption

Backup encryption is a security best practice that helps protect your organization’s confidential information and prevents unauthorized access.

The pgBackRest tool used by the Operator allows encrypting backups using AES-256 encryption. The approach is **repository-based**: pgBackRest encrypts the whole repository where it stores backups. Encryption is enabled if a user-supplied encryption key was passed to pgBackRest with the `-repo-cypher-pass` option *when configuring the backup storage*.

*Limitation:* You cannot change encryption settings after the backups are established. You must create a new repository to enable encryption or change the encryption key.

This document describes how to configure backup encryption.

## Generate the encryption key

You should use a long, random encryption key. You can generate it using OpenSSL as follows:

```
openssl rand -base64 48
```

## Configure backup storage

Follow the general [backup storage configuration](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/backups-storage.html#storage-setup-guides) instruction relevant to the backup storage you are using. The only difference is in encoding your cloud credentials and the pgBackRest repository name to be used for backups: you also add the encryption key to the configuration file as the `repo-cipher-pass` option. The repo name within the option must match the pgBackRest repo name.

The following example shows the configuration for S3-compatible storage and the pgBackRest repo name `repo2` (other cloud storages are configured similarly).

1. Encode the storage configuration file.

   **Linux**

   ```
   cat <<EOF | base64 --wrap=0
   [global]
   repo2-s3-key=<YOUR_AWS_S3_KEY>
   repo2-s3-key-secret=<YOUR_AWS_S3_KEY_SECRET>
   repo2-cipher-pass=<YOUR_ENCRYPTION_KEY>
   EOF
   ```

   **macOS**

   ```
   cat <<EOF | base64
   [global]
   repo2-s3-key=<YOUR_AWS_S3_KEY>
   repo2-s3-key-secret=<YOUR_AWS_S3_KEY_SECRET>
   repo2-cipher-pass=<YOUR_ENCRYPTION_KEY>
   EOF
   ```

1. Create the Secrets configuration file and the Secrets object following steps 2-3 of the [S3-compatible backup storage configuration](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/backups-storage-s3.html#__tabbed_1_1). For other storage types, consult the [relevant configuration tutorial](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/backups-storage.html#storage-setup-guides).

1. Update the `deploy/cr.yaml` configuration. Specify the following information:

   - The Secret name you created in the `backups.pgbackrest.configuration` subsection
   - All storage-related information in the `backups.pgbackrest.repos` subsection under the repository name that you intend to use for backups. This name must match the name you used when you encoded S3 credentials on step 1.
   - The cipher type in the `pgbackrest.global` subsection

   The following example shows the configuration for the S3-compatible storage and the pgBackRest repo name `repo2`:

   ```
   backups:
     pgbackrest:
       ...
       configuration:
         - secret:
             name: cluster1-pgbackrest-secrets
       ...
       repos:
       - name: repo2
         s3:
           bucket: "<YOUR_AWS_S3_BUCKET_NAME>"
           endpoint: "<YOUR_AWS_S3_ENDPOINT>"
           region: "<YOUR_AWS_S3_REGION>"
       global:
         cipher-type: aes-256-cbc
   ```

1. Apply the changes. Replace the `<namespace>` placeholder with your value.

   ```
   kubectl apply -f deploy/cr.yaml -n <namespace>
   ```

## Make a backup

[Make an on-demand backup](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/backups-ondemand.html) [Make a scheduled backup](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/backups-schedule.html)

# Speed-up backups with pgBackRest asynchronous archiving

Backing up a database with high write-ahead logs (WAL) generation can be rather slow, because PostgreSQL archiving process is sequential, without any parallelism or batching. In extreme cases backup can be even considered unsuccessful by the Operator because of the timeout.

The pgBackRest tool used by the Operator solves this problem by using the [WAL asynchronous archiving](https://pgbackrest.org/user-guide-centos7.html#async-archiving) feature.

Asynchronous archiving is enabled by default in the `pgBackRest` configuration. It requires the spool path to store transient data. The spool path may differ depending on the image and version. An example spool path is `/pgdata/pgbackrest-spool`.

You can further fine-tune asynchronous archiving by setting the max number of parallel processes for `archive-push` and `archive-get` commands.

Be sure not to set a high `process-max` value because it may affect normal database operations.

Your storage configuration file may look as follows:

s3.conf

```
[global]
repo2-s3-key=REPLACE-WITH-AWS-ACCESS-KEY
repo2-s3-key-secret=REPLACE-WITH-AWS-SECRET-KEY
repo2-storage-verify-tls=n
repo2-s3-uri-style=path

[global:archive-get]
process-max=2

[global:archive-push]
process-max=4
```

No modifications are needed aside of setting these additional parameters.

## Further reading

Find more information about WAL asynchronous archiving in:

- [pgBackRest official documentation](https://pgbackrest.org/user-guide-centos7.html#async-archiving)
- [How pgBackRest is Addressing Slow PostgreSQL WAL Archiving Using Asynchronous Feature](https://www.percona.com/blog/how-pgbackrest-is-addressing-slow-postgresql-wal-archiving-using-asynchronous-feature/) blog post.

# Backup retention

The Operator supports setting pgBackRest retention policies for full and differential backups. When a full backup expires according to the retention policy, pgBackRest cleans up all the files related to this backup and to the write-ahead log. Thus, the expiration of a full backup with some incremental backups based on it results in expiring of all these incremental backups.

You can control backup retention by the following `pgBackRest` options:

- `--<repo name>-retention-full` number of full backups to retain,
- `--<repo name>-retention-diff` number of differential backups to retain.

You can also specify retention type for full backups as `<repo name>-retention-full-type`, setting it to either `count` (the number of full backups to keep) or `time` (the number of days to keep a backup for).

You can set both backup type and retention policy for each of 4 repositories as follows.

```
backups:
    pgbackrest:
...
      global:
        repo1-retention-full: "14"
        repo1-retention-full-type: time
        ...
```

Differential retention can be set in a similar way:

```
backups:
    pgbackrest:
...
      global:
        repo1-retention-diff: "3"
        ...
```

# Delete the unneeded backup

The maximum amount of stored backups is controlled by the [retention policies](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/backup-retention.html). Older backups are automatically deleted.

Manual deleting of a previously saved backup requires not more than the backup name. This name can be taken from the list of available backups returned by the following command:

```
kubectl get pg-backup
```

When the name is known, backup can be deleted as follows:

```
kubectl delete pg-backup/<backup-name>
```

## Delete backups on cluster deletion

You can enable [`percona.com/delete-backups` finalizer](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/operator.html#finalizers-delete-backups) in the Custom Resource (turned off by default) to ensure that all backups are removed when the cluster is deleted. If the finalizer is enabled, the Operator will delete all the backups from all the configured repos on cluster deletion. Besides removing all the physical backup files, finalizer will also delete all `pg-backup` objects.

Warning

This `percona.com/delete-backups` finalizer is in tech preview state, and it is not yet recommended for production environments.

# Disable backups

The recommended approach to deploy and run the database is with the disaster recovery strategy in mind. Therefore, the Operator is designed and running with the backups enabled by default.

There are some specific use cases when you may wish to run a database without enabled backups. Disabling backups should be a conscious decision based on your data’s value and recoverability. These are example use cases where it is considered acceptable are when the data is fully disposable:

- Ephemeral development/testing environments: For clusters that are frequently torn down and rebuilt from application code or test data scripts.
- CI/CD pipeline jobs: For automated pipeline runs where the cluster’s entire lifecycle is temporary and tied to a single job.

## Key considerations before disabling backups

Before you proceed with disabling backups, here’s what you need to know and carefully assess:

1. Without backups you have no way to restore data. If by mistake you drop a table, that data is lost as you have no option to recover it.
1. You cannot clone a cluster when you [deploy a standby cluster for disaster recovery](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-streaming.html). This is because cloning is based on restoring a backup on a new cluster.
1. When you run a cluster without backups, `pgBackRest` metrics are unavailable.

## Start a new cluster with disabled backups

To deploy a new cluster without backups, do the following:

1. Clone the Operator repository to be able to edit resource manifests.

   ```
   git clone -b v3.1.0 https://github.com/percona/percona-postgresql-operator
   ```

1. Edit the `deploy/cr.yaml` Custom Resource and set the `backups.enabled` option to `false`

   ```
   spec:
     backups:
       enabled: false
   ```

1. Apply the Custom Resource to start the cluster creation.

   ```
   kubectl apply -f deploy/cr.yaml -n <namespace>
   ```

### Disable backups for a running cluster

Before you start, read the [considerations](#key-considerations-before-disabling-backups) carefully.

To disable backups for a running cluster, update the `deploy/cr.yaml` Custom Resource manifest with the following configuration:

- Set the `backups.enabled` option to `false`
- Add the annotation `pgv2.percona.com/authorizeBackupRemoval:"true"`

Since it is a running cluster, we will use the `kubectl patch` command to update its configuration:

```
kubectl patch pg cluster1 --type merge \
  -p '{
    "metadata": {
      "annotations": {
        "pgv2.percona.com/authorizeBackupRemoval": "true"
      }
    },
    "spec": {
      "backups": {
        "enabled": false
      }
    }
  }' -n <namespace>
```

Warning

After you apply this configuration and disable backups, the Operator deletes the `repo-host` PVC. Thus, all data that was stored in that PVC will be deleted too. The backups stored on the cloud backup storage remain.

### Re-enable backups

To re-enable backups for a running cluster, do the following:

1. Remove the annotation `pgv2.percona.com/authorizeBackupRemoval:"true"`

   ```
   kubectl annotate pg cluster1 pgv2.percona.com/authorizeBackupRemoval-
   ```

1. Apply the patch to your running cluster and enable backups:

   ```
   kubectl patch pg cluster1 --type merge \
     -p '{
       "spec": {
         "backups": {
           "enabled": true
         }
       }
     }'
   ```

# Deploy a standby cluster for Disaster Recovery

A standby cluster is a special type of PostgreSQL cluster designed to maintain a continually updated, read-only copy of your primary PostgreSQL cluster. A standby cluster applies changes made on the primary cluster either through backups or streaming replication. This ensures you always have an up-to-date replica ready to take over if the primary becomes unavailable.

In disaster recovery scenarios, standby clusters are invaluable. They let you minimize downtime and data loss by quickly promoting the standby to a writable primary when needed. This is especially important in multi-cloud or multi-regional environments, where your PostgreSQL workloads may span across various platforms and geographies.

The Percona Operator for PostgreSQL makes it straightforward to deploy and manage standby clusters on Kubernetes. By automating complex tasks and integrating tightly with Kubernetes, the operator helps you protect critical data and achieve high availability, while simplifying your operational experience.

## Types of standby clusters

You can use the Percona Operator for PostgreSQL to set up several types of standby clusters, each suited to different recovery strategies:

1. A repo-based standby that recovers WAL files from a `pgBackRest` repo stored in external storage. For this setup, you reference the `pgBackRest` repo name and the cloud-based backup configuration that matches the one from the primary site. Refer to the [Standby cluster deployment based on pgBackRest](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-backup.html) tutorial for the setup steps.
1. A streaming standby receives WAL files by connecting to the primary over the network. The primary site must be accessible over the network and allow secure authentication with TLS. The standby cluster must securely authenticate to the primary. For this reason, the custom TLS certificates of both sites must be signed by the same certificate authority (CA). For the setup, you provide the host and port of the primary cluster and the certificates. Learn more about the setup in the [Standby cluster deployment based on streaming replication](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-streaming.html) tutorial.
1. Streaming standby with external repository is the combination of two previous types and is configured with the options from both types. In this setup, the standby cluster streams WAL records from the primary. If the streaming replication falls behind, the cluster recovers WAL from the backup repo.

While a standby cluster is read-only, its pgBouncer can’t log in to PostgreSQL, so applications can’t connect through it. Connect to the database Service of the standby directly instead. In a repo-based standby, pgBouncer starts working after you promote the cluster.

## Recovery point objective

How much data you lose when the Main site is gone depends on the standby type.

A repo-based standby receives WAL only through the pgBackRest repository. PostgreSQL archives a WAL segment when it fills or after `archive_timeout`, whichever comes first. The Operator sets `archive_timeout` to 60 seconds by default. If you lose the Main site, you can lose the last 60 seconds of writes plus the time that archiving takes to reach the repository.

A standby that also streams loses only what had not yet streamed, usually seconds.

To shorten the window for a repo-based standby, lower `archive_timeout` on the Main site. The Operator lets you override it under `patroni.dynamicConfiguration.postgresql.parameters`. See [PostgreSQL parameters that can be overridden](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/immutable-options.html#postgresql-parameters-that-can-be-overridden).

```
spec:
  patroni:
    dynamicConfiguration:
      postgresql:
        parameters:
          archive_timeout: 15s
```

The change applies without restarting the database Pods. A lower value creates more WAL segments in the repository. It also makes the lag of a repo-based standby jump more often, as described in [Choose the lag threshold](#choose-the-lag-threshold).

## Detect replication lag for standby cluster

If your primary cluster has a large volume of WAL files, the standby cluster may not be able to apply them quickly enough. This may cause the standby to fall behind. This lag can result in replication issues and temporarily leave some data unavailable on the standby cluster.

You can enable replication lag detection for any standby type by setting the [`standby.maxAcceptableLag`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/operator.html#standbymaxacceptablelag) option in the Custom Resource.

### How replication lag is detected and handled

The Operator checks the WAL source based on the standby type: from the primary site or from an external repository.

For a standby cluster configured with both streaming and external repository, the Operator detects the replication lag as follows:

1. The Operator first attempts to check streaming replication lag.
1. If it fails to retrieve the streaming lag, the Operator falls back to checking the WAL replication lag from an external pgBackRest repository. Note the [known limitation for the repo-based standby](#known-limitation-for-a-repo-based-standby-cluster).
1. If streaming lag is successfully detected, this value is used.

When the WAL lag exceeds the value you specified in the `standby.maxAcceptableLag` option, the following occurs:

- The primary pod in the standby cluster is marked as `Unready`
- The cluster goes into the `initializing` state
- The `StandbyLagging` condition is set in the cluster status. You can check the conditions with the `kubectl describe pg <cluster-name> -n <namespace>` command. See [Custom resource statuses](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/cr-statuses.html#conditions) for the full list of conditions.

### Monitor lag in the cluster status

When lag detection is enabled, the cluster status includes a `standby` section that shows the current lag and when it was last computed. Use `kubectl get pg <cluster-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml` and look at `status.standby`:

```
status:
  standby:
    lagBytes: 2343212
    lagLastComputedAt: "2026-02-24T12:07:05Z"
```

- `lagBytes` — the current WAL lag in bytes (if any)
- `lagLastComputedAt` — the timestamp of the last lag check

This helps you understand if replication is lagging or broken. By surfacing the standby lag condition, you get a clear signal when your standby is not ready to serve traffic, enabling faster troubleshooting and preventing application downtime during disaster recovery scenarios.

### Known limitation for a repo-based standby cluster

For WAL lag detection to work in this standby type, the Operator must find the Main site. It looks for a cluster that is not a standby and uses the same pgBackRest repository. Therefore, WAL lag detection is available in these setups:

- Primary and standby clusters are deployed in the same namespace
- Primary and standby are deployed in different namespaces of the same cluster and the Operator is installed in cluster-wide mode.

If the Operator can’t find the Main site, for example when it runs in another Kubernetes cluster, the `StandbyLagging` condition is `Unknown` with the reason `MainSiteNotFound`, and no lag limit is enforced. The standby stays ready. To check the condition, run:

```
kubectl get pg <cluster-name> -n <namespace> \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="StandbyLagging")]}'
```

### Choose the lag threshold

The lag of a repo-based standby is the amount of WAL that the Main site wrote and the standby has not yet replayed. It includes the WAL that is not archived yet. The standby replays WAL only when it fetches a whole segment from the repository, so the lag grows until the next segment is archived.

Every time the Main site switches to a new WAL segment, the lag can briefly jump by up to one segment (16 MiB) even when the write load is low. Set `standby.maxAcceptableLag` above 16 MiB plus the amount of WAL that the Main site writes during `archive_timeout`. For a light workload, `32Mi` to `64Mi` is a reasonable start. A value below 16 MiB marks the standby as unready on routine segment switches.

The Operator checks the lag every 5 minutes, or every minute while the standby is lagging. A new `maxAcceptableLag` value applies at the next check.

### Disable replication lag detection

To disable detecting the replication lag, remove the `standby.maxAcceptableLag` from the Custom Resource. The changes apply without restarting the database Pods.

# Standby cluster deployment based on pgBackRest

The pgBackRest repo-based standby is the simplest one. The following is the architecture diagram:

## pgBackrest repo based standby

1. This solution describes two Kubernetes clusters in different regions, clouds or running in hybrid mode (on-premises and cloud). One cluster is Main and the other is Disaster Recovery (DR)

1. Each cluster includes the following components:

   1. Percona Operator
   1. PostgreSQL cluster
   1. pgBackrest
   1. pgBouncer

1. pgBackrest on the Main site streams backups and Write Ahead Logs (WALs) to the object storage

1. pgBackrest on the DR site takes these backups and streams them to the standby cluster

## Deploy disaster recovery for PostgreSQL on Kubernetes

### Configure Main site

1. Deploy the Operator [using your favorite method](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/System-Requirements.html#installation-guidelines). Once installed, configure the Custom Resource manifest, so that pgBackrest starts using the Object Storage of your choice. Skip this step if you already have it configured.

1. Configure the `backups.pgbackrest.repos` section by adding the necessary configuration. The below example is for Google Cloud Storage (GCS):

   ```
   spec:
     backups:
       configuration:
         - secret:
             name: main-pgbackrest-secrets
       pgbackrest:
         repos:
         - name: repo1
           gcs:
             bucket: MY-BUCKET
   ```

   The `main-pgbackrest-secrets` value contains the keys for GCS. Read more about the configuration in the [backup and restore tutorial](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/backups.html).

1. Once configured, apply the custom resource:

   ```
   kubectl apply -f deploy/cr.yaml
   ```

   Expected output

   ```
   perconapgcluster.pg.percona.com/standby created
   ```

   The backups should appear in the object storage. By default pgBackrest puts them into the pgbackrest folder.

### Configure DR site

The configuration of the disaster recovery site is similar [to that of the Main site](#configure-main-site), with the difference in standby settings.

The following manifest has `standby.enabled` set to `true` and points to the `repoName` where backups are (GCS in our case). Optionally, add `standby.maxAcceptableLag` to enable [replication lag detection](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby.html#detect-replication-lag-for-standby-cluster). Check the [known limitation for this standby type](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby.html#known-limitation-for-a-repo-based-standby-cluster) and [choose the threshold](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby.html#choose-the-lag-threshold) accordingly.

```
metadata:
  name: standby
spec: 
...
  backups:
    configuration:
      - secret:
          name: standby-pgbackrest-secrets
    pgbackrest:
      repos:
      - name: repo1
        gcs:
          bucket: MY-BUCKET
  standby:
    enabled: true
    repoName: repo1
    # maxAcceptableLag: 64Mi  # optional: enables replication lag detection
```

Deploy the standby cluster by applying the manifest:

```
kubectl apply -f deploy/cr.yaml
```

Expected output

```
perconapgcluster.pg.percona.com/standby created
```

### Copy the user and pgBouncer passwords

After you deploy the standby, copy the user passwords and the pgBouncer password from the Main site to the DR site, so that applications and pgBouncer can log in after you promote the DR cluster. Follow [Prepare the user passwords](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-failover.html#prepare-the-user-passwords).

# Standby cluster deployment based on streaming replication

The following diagram explains how the standby based on streaming replication works:

1. This solution describes two Kubernetes clusters in different regions, clouds, data centers or even two namespaces, or running in hybrid mode (on-premises and cloud). One cluster is Main site, and the other is Disaster Recovery site (DR)
1. Each site supposedly includes Percona Operator and for sure includes PostgreSQL cluster.
1. In the DR site the cluster is in Standby mode
1. We set up streaming replication between these two clusters

## Deploy disaster recovery for PostgreSQL on Kubernetes

### Configure Main site

1. Deploy the Operator [using your favorite method](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/System-Requirements.html#installation-guidelines).

1. The Main cluster needs to expose it, so that standby can connect to the primary PostgreSQL instance. To expose the primary PostgreSQL instance, use the `spec.expose` section:

   ```
   spec:
     ...
     expose:
       type: ClusterIP
   ```

   Use here a Service type of your choice. For example, `ClusterIP` is sufficient for two clusters in different Kubernetes namespaces.

1. Once configured, apply the custom resource:

   ```
   kubectl apply -f deploy/cr.yaml -n main-pg
   ```

   Expected output

   ```
   perconapgcluster.pg.percona.com/standby created
   ```

   The service that you should use for connecting to standby is called -ha (main-ha in my case):

   ```
   main-ha          ClusterIP   10.118.227.214   <none>        5432/TCP   163m
   ```

### Configure DR site

To get the replication working, the Standby cluster would need to authenticate with the Main one. To get there, both clusters must have certificates signed by the same certificate authority (CA). Default replication user `_crunchyrepl` will be used.

To ensure authentication, choose one of these options for the server certificate:

- **One shared server certificate.** Create one server certificate that contains the Service names of both sites, and use it on both clusters. Copy the Secrets with the certificates from the Main site to the DR namespace. Reissue the server certificate first, so that it contains the DR names, and apply it to the Main site too. This option needs the fewest certificates.
- **A server certificate for each site.** Create a separate server certificate for the DR site, with the names of the DR site only, and sign it with the same CA that signed the certificates of the Main site. The Main site keeps its server certificate.

Follow these rules when you generate the certificates:

1. Certificates for both Main and Standby clusters must be signed by the same CA. The replication user needs this to authenticate with the Main site, and the same CA lets each site trust the other after a [role swap](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-switchover.html).
1. `customReplicationTLSSecret` must have a Common Name (CN) setting that matches `_crunchyrepl`, which is a default replication user.
1. The server certificate of each site must contain the names of its own `<cluster>-primary` and `<cluster>-replicas` Services, each as `<name>`, `<name>.<namespace>`, `<name>.<namespace>.svc` and `<name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`. A shared certificate contains the names of both sites. pgBouncer checks the `<cluster>-primary` name of its own cluster. If the certificate has only the names of the Main site, pgBouncer on the DR site can’t connect to PostgreSQL after a promotion, and its log shows `name 'dr-primary' not present in server certificate`.

Create the Secrets in the namespace where the DR cluster is going to run, and reference them under `spec.secrets`:

```
spec:
  secrets:
    customTLSSecret:
      name: dr-cluster-cert
    customReplicationTLSSecret:
      name: dr-replication-cert
```

You can find more about certificates in the [TLS doc](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/TLS.html).

Apart from setting certificates correctly, you should also set standby configuration.

```
  standby:
    enabled: true
    host: main-ha.main-pg.svc
    maxAcceptableLag: 10Mi  # optional: enables replication lag detection
```

- `standby.enabled` controls if it is a standby cluster or not
- `standby.host` must point to the primary node of a Main cluster. In this example it is a `main-ha` Service in another namespace.
- `standby.maxAcceptableLag` (optional) enables replication lag detection. When the WAL lag exceeds this value, the standby primary pod is marked as unready, the cluster goes into `initializing` state, and a `StandbyLagging` condition is set in the status.

Deploy the standby cluster by applying the manifest:

```
kubectl apply -f dr-cr.yaml -n dr-pg
```

Expected output

```
perconapgcluster.pg.percona.com/standby created
```

Once both clusters are up, you can verify that replication is working.

1. Insert some data into Main cluster
1. Connect to the DR cluster

To connect to the DR cluster, use the credentials that you used to connect to Main. This also verifies that the connection is working. You should see whatever data you have in the Main cluster in the Disaster Recovery.

### Copy the user and pgBouncer passwords

Copy the user passwords and the pgBouncer password from the Main site to the DR site, so that applications and pgBouncer can log in after you promote the DR cluster. Follow [Prepare the user passwords](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-failover.html#prepare-the-user-passwords).

## Next steps

Because the certificates of both sites are signed by the same CA, you can later [swap their roles](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-switchover.html). The Main site then follows the DR site without a rebuild.

# Failover

Promote the standby cluster when the Main site is lost, for example after an outage of its Kubernetes cluster or region. The promotion makes the standby cluster writable, and it starts to push Write Ahead Logs (WALs) to the pgBackRest repository.

Before you promote, make sure that the Main site can’t accept writes. A Main site that you can’t reach isn’t necessarily down: the network can be split, or the site can come back after the promotion. Then both clusters run as primary and accept writes. This is a [split brain](#split-brain). To avoid it, shut down or delete the Main cluster before you promote the standby cluster.

The examples on this page use the `main` cluster and the `dr` cluster from the [streaming replication tutorial](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-streaming.html). Set the namespaces of your clusters once, and you can run the commands as they are:

```
export MAIN_NAMESPACE=main-pg
export DR_NAMESPACE=dr-pg
```

## Prepare the user passwords

Do this before you promote, and preferably when you set up the standby. A standby cluster replicates the users and their passwords from the Main site. While the cluster is read-only, the Operator doesn’t apply the passwords from the Disaster Recovery (DR) cluster’s own user Secrets. When you promote the cluster, the Operator sets the password of every user in `spec.users` to the value in the DR Secret `<cluster-name>-pguser-<user-name>`. If that value differs from the Main site password, applications that use the Main site credentials can’t log in after the promotion.

If you don’t set `spec.users`, there is nothing to copy. The DR cluster creates its own default user and database and leaves the default user of the Main site untouched, so the Main site credentials keep working.

For each user that you define in `spec.users`, copy the password from the Main site Secret to the DR Secret:

```
PASSWORD_B64=$(kubectl get secret main-pguser-<user-name> -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.password}')

kubectl patch secret dr-pguser-<user-name> -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}" \
  -p "{\"data\":{\"password\":\"${PASSWORD_B64}\"},\"stringData\":{\"verifier\":\"\"}}"
```

The command copies the encoded value as it is, so passwords with quotes, backslashes or non-ASCII characters stay intact. The Operator rebuilds the `verifier` from the new password within a few seconds.

The Operator creates the DR Secret together with the DR cluster, so you can run these commands right after you deploy the standby. The change takes effect when you promote the cluster.

### Copy the pgBouncer password

pgBouncer logs in to PostgreSQL as the `_crunchypgbouncer` user. Its password is in the Secret `<cluster-name>-pgbouncer`. When you promote the DR cluster, the Operator applies this user from the DR Secret, in the same way as the other users. Therefore, copy the pgBouncer password from the Main site to the DR site, so that both sites use the same one. This ensures that pgBouncer can authenticate in the new primary:

```
PGBOUNCER_PASSWORD_B64=$(kubectl get secret main-pgbouncer -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.pgbouncer-password}')

PGBOUNCER_VERIFIER_B64=$(kubectl get secret main-pgbouncer -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.pgbouncer-verifier}')

kubectl patch secret dr-pgbouncer -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}" \
  -p "{\"data\":{\"pgbouncer-password\":\"${PGBOUNCER_PASSWORD_B64}\",\"pgbouncer-verifier\":\"${PGBOUNCER_VERIFIER_B64}\"}}"
```

Copy the password and the verifier together. If you copy only the password, the Operator applies the old DR verifier when it promotes the cluster, and pgBouncer can’t log in after you swap back. Don’t set the verifier to an empty string, as you do for the user Secrets. The Operator then generates a new pgBouncer password and discards the one that you copied.

Repeat the copy after you change a password on the Main site. Clear the verifier after a promotion only if the passwords on the two sites differ. If they differ, for example because a password changed on one site after you copied it, see [Swap back](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-switchover.html#swap-back).

## Promote the standby

Once the primary is down or inactive, promote the standby through changing the corresponding section:

```
spec:
  standby:
    enabled: false
```

You can leave the other `standby` options, such as `host` and `repoName`, in the Custom Resource. The Operator ignores them when `standby.enabled` is `false`. They apply again if you set `enabled` back to `true`.

Check that `SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();` returns `f`. Now you can start writing to the cluster.

The cluster status is `ready` before and during the promotion, so don’t use it as a signal. About 10 seconds after the promotion, the Operator applies the user passwords from the DR Secrets. Applications that connect through pgBouncer can fail to log in for up to 30 seconds.

The Operator doesn’t run scheduled backups while the cluster is a standby, and starts them after the promotion.

If both sites are healthy and you want to exchange their roles, follow [Swap roles between the Main and DR sites](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-switchover.html) instead. A planned swap loses no data.

## Split brain

Split brain means that both clusters run as primary and accept writes. It happens when you promote the standby while the Main site is still running, or when the old primary comes back after you promoted the standby.

The Operator doesn’t detect it. Both clusters stay `ready` and no condition or event is set. If the standby uses the same pgBackRest repository as the Main site, archiving also reports no failures, because both clusters successfully push WAL to the same repository on diverging timelines.

### Detect split brain

Run these checks on both sites. First, get the primary Pod of each cluster:

```
MAIN_PRIMARY=$(kubectl get pod -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" \
  -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=main,postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/role=primary \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')

DR_PRIMARY=$(kubectl get pod -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}" \
  -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=dr,postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/role=primary \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
```

1. Check that no more than one cluster is writable. In a split brain, `pg_is_in_recovery()` returns `f` on both:

   ```
   kubectl exec -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" "${MAIN_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     psql -t -A -c "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();"

   kubectl exec -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}" "${DR_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     psql -t -A -c "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();"
   ```

1. Check the Patroni state. In a split brain, each site lists its own `Leader`. The `TL` (timeline) column usually differs, but both sites can also stay on the same timeline:

   ```
   kubectl exec -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" "${MAIN_PRIMARY}" -c database -- patronictl list

   kubectl exec -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}" "${DR_PRIMARY}" -c database -- patronictl list
   ```

1. For a repo-based standby and for a streaming standby with a repository, both sites may use the same pgBackRest repository. This this case, check whether the old primary still writes WAL to it. Use this check when you can’t reach the Main site. `pgbackrest info` isn’t enough. After a promotion, it lists the backup that the Operator takes after the promotion, whether the old primary still runs or not, and it doesn’t show which site wrote the WAL. First, list the WAL directories. The output has one directory for each PostgreSQL version, for example `18-1`:

   ```
   kubectl exec -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}" "${DR_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     pgbackrest --stanza=db repo-ls archive/db
   ```

   Then list the WAL files of the timeline that the Main site was on, twice, a minute apart. The first 8 characters of the directory name are the timeline, so `0000000100000000` is timeline 1:

   ```
   kubectl exec -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}" "${DR_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     pgbackrest --stanza=db repo-ls archive/db/<version-directory>/0000000100000000
   ```

   If new files appear on that timeline after the promotion, the old primary still writes. The absence of new files doesn’t prove that the Main site is down, because an idle primary may not archive new WAL. If both sites stay on the same timeline, new files can come from either site, and this check can’t tell them apart. This check doesn’t apply to a streaming standby without a repository.

Checks 1 and 2 are the reliable ones when you can reach both sites. The cluster status from `kubectl get pg` and the `pg_stat_archiver` view don’t show a split brain.

### Recover from split brain

The recovery steps depend on the type of your [standby cluster](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby.html#types-of-standby-clusters):

- For a repo-based standby and for a streaming standby with a repository, both sites share the pgBackRest repository. Follow [Recover a repo-based standby or a streaming standby with a repository](#recover-a-repo-based-standby-or-a-streaming-standby-with-a-repository).
- For a streaming standby without a repository, follow [Recover a streaming standby without a repository](#recover-a-streaming-standby-without-a-repository).

In both cases, you choose the cluster that keeps being the Main site, stop the writes to the other cluster, and rebuild the other cluster as a standby of the kept one.

The examples keep the `main` cluster and rebuild the `dr` cluster. If you keep the DR cluster, exchange the cluster names and the namespace variables. Get the primary Pod of each cluster first, as in [Detect split brain](#detect-split-brain).

#### Recover a repo-based standby or a streaming standby with a repository

Taking a new full backup from one cluster isn’t enough. The repository keeps the history and the WAL of the other timeline, so every restore and every new standby that uses the latest backup tries to follow the wrong timeline and fails.

To recover, move the cluster that you keep to a new repository path, create a full backup there, and recreate the other cluster with that path. The old repository path stays untouched, so you keep its history.

1. Stop the application writes to the other cluster, and export the rows that it accepted after the split. The writes that the kept cluster doesn’t have are the rows that were written after you promoted the standby cluster. Select them with a column that records the time or the order of the writes. The example exports one table to a file on your computer:

   ```
   kubectl exec -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}" "${DR_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     psql -d <database-name> -c "COPY (SELECT <columns> FROM <table-name> WHERE created_at >= '<promotion-time>') TO STDOUT WITH CSV HEADER" \
     > <table-name>.csv
   ```

   Repeat the command for each table that has new rows. Then pause the other cluster, so that it stops accepting writes:

   ```
   kubectl patch pg dr -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}" --type=merge \
     -p '{"spec":{"pause":true}}'
   ```

   You can delete the cluster instead. In this case, only its PVCs are left to delete.

1. Set a new, unused repository path on the kept cluster:

   ```
   kubectl patch pg main -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" --type=merge \
     -p '{"spec":{"backups":{"pgbackrest":{"global":{"repo1-path":"/pgbackrest/main-new"}}}}}'
   ```

1. Wait until the Pod of the kept cluster uses the new path. The new path reaches the Pod with a delay of up to about a minute. Run this command until the status changes to `missing stanza path`:

   ```
   kubectl exec -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" "${MAIN_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     pgbackrest --stanza=db info
   ```

   Sample output

   ```
   stanza: db
       status: error (missing stanza path)
   ```

   If you run `stanza-create` before the status changes, it reports success for the old path and doesn’t create the stanza in the new one.

1. Create the pgBackRest stanza in the new path right away. The Operator doesn’t do it when you change `repo1-path`:

   ```
   kubectl exec -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" "${MAIN_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     pgbackrest --stanza=db stanza-create
   ```

   Warning

   Until the stanza exists in the new path, PostgreSQL still reports every WAL segment as archived, but the segments are not stored in any repository. A failure of the kept cluster in this time leaves you without those WAL files.

1. Push the current timeline history file of the kept cluster to the new path. The new path doesn’t have it yet, and a standby that restores from this path needs it to follow the timeline of the kept cluster. Get the timeline number from the `TL` column of `patronictl list`. The history file name has eight digits, for example `00000002.history` for timeline 2. Replace `<version>` with your PostgreSQL major version:

   ```
   kubectl exec -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" "${MAIN_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     pgbackrest --stanza=db --no-archive-async archive-push /pgdata/pg<version>/pg_wal/<history-file>
   ```

   If the kept cluster is on timeline 1, it has no history file. Skip this step.

1. Create a full backup in the new path. Save this manifest as `deploy/backup.yaml`:

   ```
   apiVersion: pgv2.percona.com/v2
   kind: PerconaPGBackup
   metadata:
     name: after-split-brain
   spec:
     pgCluster: main
     repoName: repo1
     options:
       - --type=full
   ```

   Apply the manifest and wait for the backup to complete:

   ```
   kubectl apply -f deploy/backup.yaml -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}"

   kubectl wait perconapgbackup/after-split-brain -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" \
     --for=jsonpath='{.status.state}'=Succeeded \
     --timeout=600s
   ```

1. Delete the other cluster and its PVCs, then create it again with the same `repo1-path` as the kept cluster:

   ```
   kubectl delete pg dr -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}"

   kubectl delete pvc -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}" \
     -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=dr
   ```

   Apply the manifest of the cluster again with the new path. Keep the other options of your standby, such as `repoName`. For a streaming standby with a repository, also keep `host` and `port`, and point `host` to the `-ha` Service of the kept cluster:

   ```
   spec:
     backups:
       pgbackrest:
         global:
           repo1-path: /pgbackrest/main-new
     standby:
       enabled: true
       repoName: repo1
   ```

   The Operator restores the data from the new path as a standby of the kept cluster. The user and pgBouncer Secrets stay in the namespace, so the passwords don’t change. Check that every member is on the timeline of the kept cluster. Get a Pod of the rebuilt cluster, then run:

   ```
   kubectl exec -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}" <dr-pod-name> -c database -- patronictl list
   ```

1. Import the exported rows into the kept cluster:

   ```
   kubectl exec -i -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" "${MAIN_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     psql -d <database-name> -c "COPY <table-name> (<columns>) FROM STDIN WITH CSV HEADER" \
     < <table-name>.csv
   ```

   Both clusters kept counting from the same sequence values, so the exported rows can have the same primary keys as existing rows. Leave the primary key column out of `<columns>` in both the export and the import, so that the kept cluster assigns new keys.

1. Keep the old repository path as long as you need its history for point-in-time recovery or for an investigation. Then delete it from your storage.

Removing the other timeline’s files from the repository by hand also works, but it needs several manual deletions in the repository. A mistake destroys the history of the cluster that you keep, so this guide doesn’t cover it.

#### Recover a streaming standby without a repository

Delete the cluster that you don’t keep, together with its volumes, and create it again as a streaming standby of the kept cluster. A streaming standby without a repository can’t restore from a backup, so deleting only its PVCs and Pods doesn’t work. The new Pod waits forever with `waiting for standby_leader to bootstrap`.

1. Choose the cluster to keep. Stop the application writes to the other cluster, and export the rows that it accepted after the split.

   The other cluster loses these writes, because you delete its volumes in the next step. The writes that the kept cluster doesn’t have are the rows that were written after you promoted the standby cluster. The cluster is still writable, so you can read its tables right away. Select the rows with a column that records the time or the order of the writes. The example exports one table to a file on your computer:

   ```
   kubectl exec -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}" "${DR_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     psql -d <database-name> -c "COPY (SELECT <columns> FROM <table-name> WHERE created_at >= '<promotion-time>') TO STDOUT WITH CSV HEADER" \
     > <table-name>.csv
   ```

   Repeat the command for each table that has new rows.

1. Delete the other cluster and its PVCs:

   ```
   kubectl delete pg dr -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}"

   kubectl delete pvc -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}" \
     -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=dr
   ```

1. Create the cluster again as a streaming standby of the kept cluster. Set `standby.host` to the `-ha` Service of the kept cluster and `standby.port` to `5432`:

   ```
   spec:
     standby:
       enabled: true
       host: main-ha.main-pg.svc
       port: 5432
   ```

   The deletion keeps the user Secrets, the pgBouncer Secret and your TLS Secrets, so the new standby uses them again. If you deleted them, create the TLS Secrets again before you apply the manifest, as in [Configure DR site](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-streaming.html#configure-dr-site). Without them, the cluster doesn’t start. Then copy the user and pgBouncer passwords from the kept cluster again, as in [Prepare the user passwords](#prepare-the-user-passwords). Otherwise, pgBouncer on the new standby can’t log in to PostgreSQL after a promotion.

1. Check that the new standby is on the timeline of the kept cluster. Get a Pod of the rebuilt cluster, then run:

   ```
   kubectl exec -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}" <dr-pod-name> -c database -- patronictl list
   ```

   The member shows as `Standby Leader` in the `streaming` state, and the `TL` column has the same value as the kept cluster.

## Automate the failover

Automated failover consists of multiple steps and is outside of the Operator’s scope. There are a few steps that you can take to reduce the Recovery Time Objective (RTO). To detect the failover we recommend having the 3rd site to monitor both DR and Main sites. In this case you can be sure that Main really failed and it is not a network split situation.

Another aspect of automation is to switch the traffic for the application from Main to Standby after promotion. It can be done through various Kubernetes configurations and heavily depends on how your networking and application are designed. The following options are quite common:

1. Global Load Balancer - various clouds and vendors provide their solutions
1. Multi Cluster Services or MCS - available on most of the public clouds
1. Federation or other multi-cluster solutions

# Swap roles between the Main and DR sites

A planned switchover turns the DR site into the primary and the Main site into the standby, while both sites stay healthy. Use it for maintenance, for a disaster recovery drill, or to move the primary to another region. If the Main site is already lost, [promote the standby](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-failover.html) instead.

Stop application writes to the Main site before you start. The swap then loses no data. Writes stay unavailable for about 15 to 25 seconds, plus the time the DR site needs to replay any WAL that it hasn’t applied yet.

## What happens to the old primary

The type of your [standby cluster](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby.html#types-of-standby-clusters) decides what the Main site does after DR is promoted:

| Standby type                              | Main site after the swap                      | What you do                                                               |
| ----------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Streaming, or streaming with a repository | Follows the new primary on its own            | Nothing. Check with `patronictl list`                                     |
| Repo-based                                | Stays on its old timeline and can’t follow DR | [Rebuild the Main site](#rebuild-the-old-primary-of-a-repo-based-standby) |

A repository-based Main site cannot follow because the shutdown checkpoint never reaches the pgBackRest repository. This checkpoint is the final record that PostgreSQL writes when it stops. The DR site never replays that record, so the two sites end up on different timelines. If you plan regular swaps, use a streaming standby and avoid the rebuild.

## Before you start

The examples use the `main` cluster and the `dr` cluster from the [streaming replication tutorial](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-streaming.html). Set the namespaces of your clusters once, and you can run the commands as they are:

```
export MAIN_NAMESPACE=main-pg
export DR_NAMESPACE=dr-pg
```

1. Check that the DR cluster is `ready` and that the `StandbyLagging` condition isn’t `True`:

   ```
   kubectl get pg dr -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}"
   ```

1. For a streaming standby, check that the Main site can reach the DR `-ha` Service and trusts its certificates. The certificates of both sites must be [signed by the same CA](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-streaming.html#configure-dr-site).

1. Make sure that the DR cluster has the same user passwords and the same pgBouncer password as the Main site. When the Operator promotes DR, it sets the password of each user in `spec.users` and of the pgBouncer user to the value in the DR Secret. Follow [Prepare the user passwords](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-failover.html#prepare-the-user-passwords) for each user, and [Copy the pgBouncer password](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-failover.html#copy-the-pgbouncer-password). When the passwords are the same on both sites, pgBouncer can authenticate in the new primary. If the passwords differ, see [Swap back](#swap-back).

1. Make sure you can switch application traffic to the DR site after the swap.

## Swap the roles

1. Stop application writes to the Main site.

   The Operator doesn’t stop two clusters from running as primary at the same time. Writes that both sites accept during an overlap are lost on the site that you demote.

1. Get the Main primary Pod and record its current WAL position:

   ```
   MAIN_PRIMARY=$(kubectl get pod -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" \
     -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=main,postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/role=primary \
     -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')

   kubectl exec -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" "${MAIN_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     psql -t -A -c "SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();"
   ```

   Sample output

   ```
   0/7034CF8
   ```

   Save this value. Read it after you stop the writes and before you demote the Main site. A value that you read after the demotion is never reached by a repo-based standby, and the wait in step 5 never ends.

   You don’t need to run `pg_switch_wal()`. When the Main site shuts down cleanly during the demotion, PostgreSQL switches to a new WAL segment and archives it, so the DR site receives all the writes.

1. Demote the Main site. Set `standby.enabled` to `true` and point the cluster to the repository. For a streaming standby, also set `standby.host` to the DR `-ha` Service:

   **Repo-based standby**

   ```
   kubectl patch pg main -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" --type=merge \
     -p '{"spec":{"standby":{"enabled":true,"repoName":"repo1","host":null,"port":null}}}'
   ```

   The `null` values remove a `host` that the cluster kept from an earlier standby setup, so that the Main site reads only from the repository.

   **Streaming standby**

   ```
   kubectl patch pg main -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" --type=merge \
     -p "{\"spec\":{\"standby\":{\"enabled\":true,\"repoName\":\"repo1\",\"host\":\"dr-ha.${DR_NAMESPACE}.svc\",\"port\":5432}}}"
   ```

   If your standby has no repository, omit `repoName`.

1. Wait for the Main site to stop accepting writes:

   ```
   kubectl exec -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" "${MAIN_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     psql -t -A -c "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();"
   ```

   Don’t continue until the command returns `t`.

1. Wait until the DR site replays the position that you recorded in step 2. Get the DR primary Pod, then run the check until it returns `t`. Replace `<lsn>` with the saved value:

   ```
   DR_PRIMARY=$(kubectl get pod -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}" \
     -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=dr,postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/role=primary \
     -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')

   kubectl exec -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}" "${DR_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     psql -t -A -c "SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= '<lsn>'::pg_lsn;"
   ```

   A repo-based standby replays WAL when it fetches a segment from the repository, so this step can take several seconds.

1. Promote the DR site:

   ```
   kubectl patch pg dr -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}" --type=merge \
     -p '{"spec":{"standby":{"enabled":false}}}'
   ```

1. Confirm that the DR site accepts writes:

   ```
   kubectl exec -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}" "${DR_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     psql -t -A -c "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();"
   ```

   The command returns `f`. Switch your applications to the DR site. The Operator applies the user passwords about 10 seconds later. If your applications connect through pgBouncer, they can fail to log in for up to 30 seconds.

1. Check the Main site. For a streaming standby, `patronictl list` shows the Main member as `Standby Leader` in the `streaming` state on the new timeline:

   ```
   kubectl exec -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" "${MAIN_PRIMARY}" -c database -- patronictl list
   ```

   For a repo-based standby, the member stays in `in archive recovery` on the old timeline. The PostgreSQL log repeats `new timeline 2 forked off current database system timeline 1`. Rebuild the Main site as described in the next section.

## Rebuild the old primary of a repo-based standby

Choose one of these ways to bring the Main site back as a standby of DR.

### Recreate the instance

This is the simplest way. After the swap, DR is the primary and holds all the writes that the Main site acknowledged, and the Main site is a standby. The data on the Main volumes has diverged from DR, so you can discard it. The Operator creates new instances, restores the latest backup from the pgBackRest repository, and replays the WAL from the repository until the Main site catches up with DR. Restore time depends on the size of your data.

Recreate every PostgreSQL instance of the Main site. The replicas of the old primary diverge as well, even though they report `streaming` and stay ready. If you recreate only the primary, Patroni makes a diverged replica the new standby leader.

Warning

Delete the Main volumes only after the swap is complete. Check that the DR site accepts writes (step 7), that the Main site is in recovery (step 4), and that the repository has a backup:

```
kubectl exec -n "${DR_NAMESPACE}" "${DR_PRIMARY}" -c database -- pgbackrest --stanza=db info
```

If you delete the volumes of a site that is still the only primary, or before DR has replayed the recorded position in step 5, you lose data.

1. Delete the PVCs and the Pods of all Main instances:

   ```
   kubectl delete pvc -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" \
     -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=main,postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/data=postgres \
     --wait=false

   kubectl delete pod -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" \
     -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=main,postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/data=postgres
   ```

1. Check that every member is on the DR timeline:

   ```
   kubectl exec -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" <main-pod-name> -c database -- patronictl list
   ```

   All members show the same `TL` as DR: one `Standby Leader` and the replicas in the `streaming` state.

`patronictl reinit` doesn’t help here, because the Main site is a standby. On the primary it fails with `No replica among provided members`, and on the replicas it fails with `invalid option '--scope=main-ha'`.

### Add a streaming source

With a streaming source, Patroni rewinds the Main site with `pg_rewind` and no restore is needed. The Main site must trust the DR certificates. This way is for a Main site with one PostgreSQL instance. If your site has replicas, recreate every instance instead.

1. Check that the certificates of the Main site and of the DR site are signed by the same CA, as in [Configure DR site](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-streaming.html#configure-dr-site). The Main site then trusts the DR certificates, and it keeps its own certificates.

1. Set the DR `-ha` Service as the standby host of the Main cluster:

   ```
   kubectl patch pg main -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" --type=merge \
     -p "{\"spec\":{\"standby\":{\"enabled\":true,\"repoName\":\"repo1\",\"host\":\"dr-ha.${DR_NAMESPACE}.svc\",\"port\":5432}}}"
   ```

   If the Main site doesn’t trust the DR certificates, the rewind fails with `SSL error: certificate verify failed` and the Main site stays diverged.

## Swap back

The roles are now reversed, and the swap back is the same procedure with the sites exchanged. For a repo-based standby, you rebuild the DR site the same way. To avoid the rebuild, [add a streaming source](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-streaming.html) to the standby before the next swap.

### Re-apply the user passwords

Clear the verifier only if the passwords on the two sites differ. If you copied the user passwords and the pgBouncer password to both sites, and nobody changed them since, skip this section.

The Operator applies the passwords from the user Secrets of a cluster only when a Secret changes. A site that was primary before keeps the passwords that the other site set while it was primary, including a password that you changed there. The Operator doesn’t re-apply the `pgBouncer` user either, so pgBouncer on the promoted site can’t log in to PostgreSQL, unless both sites have the same pgBouncer password and verifier.

After you promote the site, clear the `verifier` in the Secret of each user, so that the Operator rebuilds it from the password in that Secret and applies it again. The example uses the Main site:

```
kubectl patch secret main-pguser-<user-name> -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" \
  -p '{"stringData":{"verifier":""}}'
```

The pgBouncer Secret works differently. If you copied the pgBouncer password and verifier between the sites, as in [Copy the pgBouncer password](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-failover.html#copy-the-pgbouncer-password), pgBouncer already works. Otherwise, clear the pgBouncer verifier. The Operator then generates a new pgBouncer password and a new verifier, and applies them:

```
kubectl patch secret main-pgbouncer -n "${MAIN_NAMESPACE}" \
  -p '{"stringData":{"pgbouncer-verifier":""}}'
```

The user passwords from the Main Secrets apply again, and logins through pgBouncer work after about a minute. The pgBouncer passwords of the two sites differ afterwards, so copy the pgBouncer password and verifier again before the next swap.

To keep a user password that you changed on the other site, copy it to the Main Secret first, as in [Prepare the user passwords](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-failover.html#prepare-the-user-passwords). For the pgBouncer password, see [Copy the pgBouncer password](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby-failover.html#copy-the-pgbouncer-password).

# Scale Percona Distribution for PostgreSQL on Kubernetes

Kubernetes makes it straightforward to give a workload more capacity: you change the Custom Resource, and the Operator reconciles Pods, compute resources and storage to match.

Scaling can be vertical or horizontal:

- **Vertical scaling** adds CPU, memory, or disk to existing PostgreSQL members.
- **Horizontal scaling** adds more PostgreSQL members to the cluster.

Adding members can look similar to [high availability](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/ha-deploy.html), but the goals differ. Scaling is about capacity while high availability is about surviving failures.

This document explains scaling. For failover, replication modes, and recommended cluster size, see [High availability](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/ha-deploy.html).

## Next steps

[Scale horizontally](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/scaling-horizontal.html) [Scale vertically](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/scaling-vertical.html)

# Scale a PostgreSQL cluster horizontally

Horizontal scaling means adding members to your PostgreSQL cluster. New members join as standbys via streaming replication.

Horizontal scaling enhances your cluster’s **read** capacity and increases the number of available failover candidates. However, it does not increase write throughput. PostgreSQL still has only **one primary** member that handles all write operations. Standbys are read-only.

You can add extra nodes in two ways:

- Change the number of replicas in the existing instance set
- Change the number of instance sets

Key concepts to understand:

- An **instance set** is one entry under `spec.instances`. Members in the same set share the same resources, storage, sidecars, and related settings. The Operator manages each PostgreSQL member as its own StatefulSet within that set.
- **`replicas`** is how many PostgreSQL members belong to that instance set. One member becomes primary; the others are standbys.

## Choose between replicas and instance sets

| Approach                       | What the Operator does                                       | Prefer when                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Increase `replicas` on one set | Adds or removes members in that instance set                 | Standard high availability and read replicas with the same settings (storage, compute resources, affinity rules) |
| Add another `instances` entry  | Creates a new instance set with its own members and settings | Different configuration or hardware, migration                                                                   |

## Add replicas in an instance set

Use this approach when you want a cluster with **identical** members for high availability or to serve more read traffic.

For example, you have three members (one primary and 2 standbys):

```
spec:
...
  instances:
    - name: instance1
      replicas: 3
```

Increase the replica count:

```
spec:
...
  instances:
    - name: instance1
      replicas: 5
```

Apply the Custom Resource:

```
kubectl apply -f deploy/cr.yaml
```

The Operator adds two more members in the same instance set. The new standbys are ready after they synchronize from the primary.

**Best practices**

- Prefer **3** members for production high availability. Two is a fragile minimum. See [High availability](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/ha-deploy.html).
- Pair scaling with [anti-affinity and topology spread](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/constraints.html) so members do not share a single Kubernetes node.
- More replicas do not increase write capacity. Only the primary accepts writes. To spread read load, connect read-only clients to the replica Service or pgBouncer. See [Exposing cluster](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/expose.html).
- Each new standby needs its own PVC and copies data from the primary. Plan for that storage and network load.
- Raise the replica count gradually. Wait until each new standby finishes syncing before you rely on it.
- If you reduce the number of replicas in the instance set, the Operator keeps the primary and removes a standby Pod. You can set the target count but you cannot define which standby Pod to remove.

## Add an extra instance set

Add another `spec.instances` entry when members need a **different** configuration, or when you want to scale one group independently of another.

Each instance set can have its own configuration for resources, storage class, sidecars, and more. The Operator creates a separate StatefulSet for each configured set. However, all these sets remain part of the same PostgreSQL/Patroni cluster and synchronize the data through replication.

Typical use cases:

- Migrate to new hardware or a new storage class
- Blue-green style rollout of a new configuration
- Try new sidecar versions or sizing next to the existing set
- Control **which group** of members you add, drain, or stop, and in which sequence you apply those Custom Resource changes.

For example, migrate from `old-ssd` to `new-ssd` while keeping the existing instance set intact:

```
spec:
...
  instances:
    - name: instance1
      replicas: 2
      dataVolumeClaimSpec:
        storageClassName: old-ssd
        accessModes:
        - ReadWriteOnce
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 100Gi
    - name: instance2
      replicas: 2
      dataVolumeClaimSpec:
        storageClassName: new-ssd
        accessModes:
        - ReadWriteOnce
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 100Gi
```

Apply the Custom Resource, wait until the new members are healthy and caught up, then scale down or remove the old instance set when you are ready.

**Best practices**

- Extra instance sets fit migration and mixed configuration. For identical members, increasing `replicas` on one set is usually simpler.
- Name instance sets clearly (for example `instance1`, `instance2-new-ssd`).
- Members in each instance set get dedicated PVC. When you deploy several instance sets, you need storage and replication capacity for all of them. Plan for that before you scale.
- Decide which set should host the primary during cutover, then remove the old set deliberately. See [Change the primary](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/change-primary.html).
- Apply [affinity and topology rules](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/constraints.html) so new members are spread across failure domains.
- Scale each set on its own: for example, bring `instance2` up first, then set `instance1` replicas to `0` or remove that entry after cutover.

# Scale a PostgreSQL cluster vertically

Vertical scaling adds CPU, memory, or disk to existing PostgreSQL members. Use it when the cluster needs more resources per Pod rather than more members. For adding members, see [Scale horizontally](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/scaling-horizontal.html).

## Scale compute resources

The Operator deploys and manages several components: PostgreSQL instances, pgBouncer, pgBackRest, and others. See [Architecture](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/architecture.html) for the full list.

You can manage CPU or memory for every component in the corresponding section of the Custom Resource. The Operator follows the Kubernetes model for [requests and limits](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/) :

- A **request** tells the scheduler how much CPU or memory the Pod needs. Kubernetes places the Pod only on a node that can satisfy every request.
- A **limit** is the maximum CPU or memory the container may use. Above the limit, the container may be throttled (CPU) or terminated (memory).

You can set both `requests` and `limits` in the `resources` section. For example:

```
spec:
...
  instances:
  - name: instance1
    replicas: 3
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: 1.0
        memory: 2Gi
      limits:
        cpu: 2.0
        memory: 4Gi
```

If you set only `limits` and omit `requests`, Kubernetes defaults the request to the limit value.

See the [Custom Resource options](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/operator.html) for other components.

## Scale storage

Kubernetes manages storage with the following components:

- a PersistentVolume (PV) - a segment of storage supplied by the Kubernetes administrator
- a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) - a request for storage from a user

Starting with Kubernetes v1.11, you can increase the size of an existing PVC object (considered stable since Kubernetes v1.24). Note that you **cannot shrink** the size of an existing PVC object.
