| [Migrate with backup and restore](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/migrate-from-crunchy-backup-restore.html) – back up data in Crunchy and restore it in Percona Operator           | - Allows test runs of the migration - The Crunchy cluster stays unchanged, so you can roll back by pointing applications back to it - Works across Kubernetes clusters that share backup storage                             | - Downtime lasts for the restore, usually minutes, and grows with the data size - Requires a backup repository in object storage. If the Crunchy cluster only has a volume repository, you must add one                                                                                          |
| [Migrate reusing data volumes](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/migrate-from-crunchy-data-volumes.html) – reuse the Persistent Volume Claims (PVCs) from a Crunchy cluster          | - No need to move large data over the network - Downtime doesn’t grow with the data size                                                                                                                                     | - Requires downtime while the volumes move to the new cluster - Requires permissions to modify PersistentVolumes, usually cluster-admin - Every volume of the primary (data, WAL, tablespaces) must move to the new cluster - Rollback is possible only from a backup taken before the migration |

# Pre-migration compatibility checks

Important

Read this before you migrate.

Complete these checks **before** you pick a migration method. Verify that source and target environments are compatible. Migration methods such as pgBackRest restore, standby replication or reusing the existing PostgreSQL data volume all reuse the source PGDATA files. For all these methods, CPU architecture and the PostgreSQL major version must match. If they don’t, migrate using `pg_dump` / `pg_restore` instead.

Differences in the operating system, libraries like `glibc`, ICU, or PostgreSQL extensions do not always block reuse of `PGDATA`. But you must take extra steps before or after the migration.

## Decide whether you can reuse the data files

Use this flow to interpret the checks. Then gather the facts in the sections that follow.

```
flowchart TD
    A[Compare PostgreSQL major versions] -->|Different| B[Do not use standby, backup/restore, or volume reuse]
    A -->|Same| C[Compare CPU architecture]
    C -->|Different| D[Prefer logical migration]
    C -->|Same| E[Compare OS / glibc / ICU]
    E -->|Same| F[Compare extensions]
    E -->|Different| G[Check collation versions]
    G -->|Match| F
    G -->|Mismatch| H[Identify affected indexes]
    H --> I[REINDEX]
    I --> J[REFRESH COLLATION VERSION]
    J --> F
    F --> K[Trial runs]
    K --> L[Fix issues if any]
    L --> M[Migrate]
    M --> N[Validate PostgreSQL and check the logs]
```

## Compare PostgreSQL major versions

The PostgreSQL major version of the source and target database images must match.

Check the source (Crunchy) PostgreSQL version:

```
kubectl exec -n <namespace> <source-postgres-pod> -c database -- \
  postgres --version
```

Sample output

```
postgres (PostgreSQL) 18.6
```

Check the version in the target Percona image as well. Find tags in [Percona certified images](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/images.html). If the Percona cluster is not running yet, start a temporary Pod from the target image:

```
kubectl run pg-image-check --rm -it --restart=Never \
  --image=<percona-postgres-image> -- \
  postgres --version
```

The major versions must match, for example:

```
Source: postgres (PostgreSQL) 18.6
Target: postgres (PostgreSQL) 18.6 - Percona Server for PostgreSQL 18.6.1
```

A difference in the minor version is normally supported by PostgreSQL’s physical storage format, but the target minor version should be equal to or newer than the source.

Do not reuse `PGDATA` or restore a physical backup directly into a different PostgreSQL major version.

## Compare CPU architecture

Check the architecture of both the source and target PostgreSQL containers:

```
kubectl exec -n <namespace> <source-postgres-pod> -c database -- uname -m
kubectl exec -n <namespace> <percona-postgres-pod> -c database -- uname -m
```

Expected output

```
x86_64
```

or:

```
aarch64
```

The source and target must use the same architecture.

For example:

```
x86_64 -> x86_64    OK
ARM64  -> ARM64     OK
x86_64 -> ARM64     Not OK
```

Use `pg_dump` / `pg_restore` when you migrate across incompatible architectures.

## Compare OS, glibc, and ICU

Run these commands against the source Crunchy pod. Repeat them against the target Percona image (use a temporary Pod if the cluster is not running yet).

### Check operating system

Check the operating system used by the PostgreSQL container:

```
kubectl exec -n <namespace> <postgres-pod> -c database -- \
  cat /etc/os-release
```

Check the `glibc` version:

```
kubectl exec -n <namespace> <postgres-pod> -c database -- \
  getconf GNU_LIBC_VERSION
```

Example:

```
glibc 2.34
```

Percona PostgreSQL images are based on [Red Hat Universal Base Image (UBI)](https://catalog.redhat.com/en/software/base-images) . Each UBI major ships a different `glibc` version:

| UBI version | glibc version |
| ----------- | ------------- |
| UBI 8       | glibc 2.28    |
| UBI 9       | glibc 2.34    |
| UBI 10      | glibc 2.39    |

Use the same UBI major for every instance in a cluster. Find image tags in [Percona certified images](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/images.html).

If the Crunchy image is UBI 8 and you use the default Percona image (UBI 9), you will see a `glibc` change:

```
Source:
  UBI 8
  glibc 2.28

Target:
  UBI 9
  glibc 2.34
```

A different `glibc` version does not by itself make the PostgreSQL data directory incompatible. `glibc` provides locale and collation rules that PostgreSQL uses. A change in these rules can make existing collation-dependent indexes inconsistent with the target operating system. See [Locale data changes](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Locale_data_changes) in the PostgreSQL wiki.

### Check ICU library version

PostgreSQL may also use ICU for collations. Check the locale provider in each database:

```
  SELECT datname, datlocprovider, datcollversion FROM pg_database;
```

Sample output

```
  datname  | datlocprovider | datcollversion
-----------+----------------+----------------
postgres  | c              | 2.34
template1 | c              | 2.34
template0 | c              |
cluster1  | c              | 2.34
(4 rows)
```

`c` is libc (`glibc`). `i` is ICU. If the provider is `i` and the source and target images ship different ICU libraries, treat that the same as a `glibc` change.

If `glibc` or ICU differs, run the collation checks **after** PostgreSQL starts on the target image. You can run the index scan on the source cluster beforehand to estimate the work.

[Connect to PostgreSQL](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/connect.html) with the privileges of the superuser or the database owner and run the following query:

```
SELECT DISTINCT
    indrelid::regclass::text,
    indexrelid::regclass::text,
    collname,
    pg_get_indexdef(indexrelid)
FROM (
    SELECT
        indexrelid,
        indrelid,
        indcollation[i] coll
    FROM
        pg_index,
        generate_subscripts(indcollation, 1) g(i)
) s
JOIN pg_collation c ON coll = c.oid
WHERE
    collprovider IN ('d', 'c')
    AND collname NOT IN ('C', 'POSIX');
```

Check indexes that rely on collations other than `C` or `POSIX` and whose collations were provided by the operating system (`c`) or dynamic libraries (`d`). If you see affected indexes, find the databases whose collation version changed:

```
SELECT datname, datlocprovider, datcollate, datcollversion
FROM pg_database;
```

Sample output

```
datname   | datlocprovider | datcollate  | datcollversion
----------+----------------+-------------+----------------
postgres  | c              | en_US.utf-8 | 2.28
template1 | c              | en_US.utf-8 | 2.28
template0 | c              | en_US.utf-8 |
cluster1  | c              | en_US.utf-8 | 2.28
```

## Compare extensions

Record the extension list and versions on the source cluster before you migrate.

Extensions are installed per database. Check every application database, not only `postgres`:

```
SELECT
    extname,
    extversion
FROM pg_extension
ORDER BY extname;
```

Sample output

```
extname             | extversion
--------------------+-----------
plpgsql             | 1.0
pg_stat_statements  | 1.12
postgis             | 3.4.2
pgcrypto            | 1.3
```

Verify that each extension is available in the target Percona image. Percona Distribution for PostgreSQL ships a defined set of tested extensions. Their versions may differ from the Crunchy image.

You can also [add custom extensions](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/custom-extensions.html#add-custom-extensions) if you need them or if they are missing in Percona images. Evaluate the risk before you add any extension.

Pay particular attention to extensions that contain native C/C++ libraries. Those extensions need a shared library in the PostgreSQL installation, not only a catalog entry in `PGDATA`. Do not assume an extension is available because it exists in `pg_extension`.

## Before you cut over

Perform at least **three successful trial runs** in a comparable test environment and validate the application after each one. The first run usually exposes missing steps, the second confirms the fixes, and the third shows that the procedure is repeatable and the cutover time is predictable. Capture that as a detailed, environment-specific runbook before you migrate production workloads.

After PostgreSQL starts under Percona Operator for PostgreSQL, check the PostgreSQL logs for errors, then confirm that collation rebuilds and extensions are complete.

# Migrate from Crunchy to Percona Operator for PostgreSQL using a standby cluster

A standby cluster is a PostgreSQL cluster that doesn’t have a writable primary. Instead, it applies changes from backups or from streaming replication from another database that acts as the source.

Using a standby cluster when migrating your PostgreSQL workloads, you maintain a live, synchronized copy of your original Crunchy cluster in Percona Operator for PostgreSQL. This approach minimizes downtime and gives you a way to validate the new cluster before switching over.

In this migration guide, we deploy Percona Operator for PostgreSQL as a standby cluster for a Crunchy PostgreSQL cluster by using a combination of backup and streaming replication. This approach ensures a fast initial data sync and keeps your data up to date with minimal downtime during cutover. For more information about standby cluster types, see [standby cluster types](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/standby.html#types-of-standby-clusters).

Then we cut over the Crunchy PostgreSQL cluster and promote Percona Operator for PostgreSQL.

This migration provides minimal downtime that happens only during the cutover.

## Versions used in this guide

For this migration tutorial, we use the following versions of the Operators:

- Crunchy PostgreSQL Operator 5.8.x
- Percona Operator for PostgreSQL 3.x.x
- An AWS S3 storage for backups. If you use another remote storage, configure access to it for both clusters.

## Before you migrate

Complete the [Pre-migration compatibility checks](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/migrate-checklist.html). Physical methods require a matching PostgreSQL major version and CPU architecture.

## Prerequisites

Ensure you have the following:

- A Kubernetes or OpenShift cluster with permissions to create namespaces, CRDs, Roles, and Deployments.
- [Helm](https://helm.sh/) 3.x.
- `kubectl` or `oc` command line tools
- [yq](https://github.com/mikefarah/yq) YAML processor.
- A remote backup storage reachable from Pods in both the Crunchy and Percona namespaces.

## Before you start

1. Create the namespaces for Crunchy Operator for PostgreSQL and Percona Operator for PostgreSQL and export them as the environment variables. If you already run Crunchy Operator for PostgreSQL, export its namespace as the environment variable.

   ```
   export CRUNCHY_NS=postgres-operator
   export NAMESPACE=pgo
   ```

1. Clone the repositories to edit the manifests during the migration setup:

   - For Crunchy PostgreSQL Operator:

   ```
   git clone https://github.com/CrunchyData/postgres-operator.git
   ```

   - For Percona Operator for PostgreSQL:

   ```
   git clone -b v3.1.0 https://github.com/percona/percona-postgresql-operator
   ```

## Deploy Crunchy Operator for PostgreSQL

Skip this step if you already run Crunchy Operator for PostgreSQL.

If you don’t, install the Operator Deployment following the [official Crunchy documentation](https://access.crunchydata.com/documentation/postgres-operator/5.8/quickstart) .

## Adapt the configuration for Crunchy PostgreSQL cluster

Whether you are deploying a new Crunchy PostgreSQL cluster or already have one running, make sure that:

1. `pgBackRest` is configured to send backups to a remote storage that will be accessible by the Percona standby cluster.
1. The Percona cluster can reach the Crunchy primary Service for streaming replication. If both clusters run in the same Kubernetes cluster, the `<clusterName>-ha` Service is reachable from other namespaces and needs no changes. If they run in different Kubernetes clusters, expose the Service outside the cluster, for example with `spec.service.type: LoadBalancer` in the `PostgresCluster` Custom Resource.

To meet these requirements, do the following:

1. Create a Secret containing the access credentials for your backup storage. This example configuration uses AWS S3 as the backup storage and the `repo1` as the `pgBackRest` repository for storing backups there:

   storage-access.yaml

   ```
   apiVersion: v1
   kind: Secret
   metadata:
     name: crunchy-pgbackrest-secret
   stringData:
     s3.conf: |
       [global]
       repo1-s3-key=<your-access-key>
       repo1-s3-key-secret=<your-access-secret>
   ```

   For more configuration examples for other storages, see [Configure backup storage](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/backups-storage.html)

1. Apply the file to create the Secret:

   ```
   kubectl apply -f storage-access.yaml -n $CRUNCHY_NS
   ```

1. Edit the `PostgresCluster` Custom Resource configuration to include the following configuration:

   For `pgBackRest` configuration:

   - The name of the Secret
   - The name of the bucket
   - The endpoint on the storage
   - The shared path for both Crunchy and Percona standby clusters

   Here’s the example configuration for Crunchy PostgreSQL cluster showing these important settings:

   postgres.yaml

   ```
   apiVersion: postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/v1beta1
   kind: PostgresCluster
   metadata:
     name: crunchy-source   
   spec:
     postgresVersion: 18
     instances:
       - name: instance1
         replicas: 3
         dataVolumeClaimSpec:
           accessModes:
             - ReadWriteOnce
           resources:
             requests:
               storage: 10Gi
     backups:
       pgbackrest:
         configuration:
           - secret:
               name: crunchy-pgbackrest-secret
         manual:
           repoName: repo1
           options:
             - --type=full
         global:
           repo1-path: /crunchy-to-percona/repo1
           repo1-s3-uri-style: path
           repo1-s3-verify-tls: "n" # Skip if you use AWS S3
         repos:
           - name: repo1
             s3:
               bucket: <YOUR_BUCKET_HERE>
               endpoint: s3.amazonaws.com
               region: <YOUR_REGION_HERE>
     proxy:
       pgBouncer:
         replicas: 1
   ```

1. Apply the configuration to create the new or update the existing Crunchy PostgreSQL cluster:

   ```
   kubectl apply -f postgres.yaml -n $CRUNCHY_NS
   ```

1. Wait until all PostgreSQL instances of the cluster are ready. Set the number to the `replicas` value of the `instance1` instance set (`3` in this example):

   ```
   kubectl wait postgrescluster.postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/crunchy-source \
     -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     --for=jsonpath='{.status.instances[?(@.name=="instance1")].readyReplicas}'=3 \
     --timeout=600s
   ```

   Expected output

   ```
   postgrescluster.postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/crunchy-source condition met
   ```

   This command waits on the cluster status, so you can run it right after `kubectl apply`. A `kubectl wait pod` command fails with `no matching resources found` if the Pods don’t exist yet.

## Make a full backup on the Crunchy PostgreSQL cluster before the migration

Make a full backup. This ensures the standby cluster has a recent restore point and needs to replay a small amount of WAL files to synchronize.

1. Start a full backup of your Crunchy PostgreSQL cluster. The annotation value identifies this backup request, so save it in a variable:

   ```
   BACKUP_ID=$(date +%s)
   kubectl annotate postgrescluster.postgres-operator.crunchydata.com crunchy-source \
     --namespace "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     --overwrite \
     postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/pgbackrest-backup="${BACKUP_ID}"
   ```

   The `--overwrite` flag lets you re-run the command if the cluster already has this annotation from an earlier backup.

1. Wait until the Crunchy Operator picks up this backup request:

   ```
   kubectl wait postgrescluster.postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/crunchy-source \
     -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     --for=jsonpath='{.status.pgbackrest.manualBackup.id}'="${BACKUP_ID}" \
     --timeout=120s
   ```

1. Wait for the backup to finish:

   ```
   kubectl wait postgrescluster.postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/crunchy-source \
     -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     --for=jsonpath='{.status.pgbackrest.manualBackup.finished}'=true \
     --timeout=600s
   ```

   On a newly created Crunchy cluster, the Crunchy Operator first completes its automatic initial backup and starts your backup only after that. The timeout covers both backups. For a large cluster, increase it.

   Expected output

   ```
   postgrescluster.postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/crunchy-source condition met
   ```

1. Check that the backup succeeded:

   ```
   kubectl get postgrescluster.postgres-operator.crunchydata.com crunchy-source \
     -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     -o jsonpath='{.status.pgbackrest.manualBackup.succeeded}{"\n"}'
   ```

   The output is `1` for a successful backup.

   If the backup fails, the Crunchy Operator retries it. During the retries, `finished` stays `false` and the previous wait times out, while `status.pgbackrest.manualBackup.failed` counts the failed attempts. Check it with:

   ```
   kubectl get postgrescluster.postgres-operator.crunchydata.com crunchy-source \
     -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     -o jsonpath='{.status.pgbackrest.manualBackup}{"\n"}'
   ```

   To find the backup Job and check its logs, run:

   ```
   kubectl get job -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=crunchy-source,postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/pgbackrest-backup=manual
   ```

   After you fix the cause, start the backup again with a new `BACKUP_ID` value.

## Export data for the standby cluster

If the Percona cluster runs in a **different** namespace than Crunchy, copy the Crunchy TLS secrets into the Percona namespace for mutual TLS on the replication connection:

1. Retrieve the Secrets:

   ```
   kubectl get secrets -n $CRUNCHY_NS
   ```

   Expected output

   ```
   crunchy-pgbackrest-secret             Opaque               1      7h29m
   crunchy-source-cluster-cert           Opaque               3      7h29m
   crunchy-source-instance1-khbq-certs   Opaque               6      7h29m
   crunchy-source-instance1-ndrp-certs   Opaque               6      7h29m
   crunchy-source-instance1-xlh6-certs   Opaque               6      7h29m
   crunchy-source-pgbackrest             Opaque               3      7h29m
   crunchy-source-pgbouncer              Opaque               6      7h29m
   crunchy-source-pguser-crunchy-source           Opaque               12     7h29m
   crunchy-source-replication-cert       Opaque               3      7h29m
   pgo-root-cacert                       Opaque               2      7h29m
   ```

   The Secrets we are interested in are `crunchy-source-cluster-cert` and `crunchy-source-replication-cert`

1. Export Secrets to a file:

   ```
   kubectl get secret crunchy-source-cluster-cert -o json -n "$CRUNCHY_NS" \
     | yq -o yaml '
   {
     "apiVersion": .apiVersion,
     "kind": .kind,
     "data": .data,
     "metadata": {"name": .metadata.name},
     "type": .type
   }
   ' > ~/crunchy-source-cluster-cert.yaml

   kubectl get secret crunchy-source-replication-cert -o json -n "$CRUNCHY_NS" \
     | yq -o yaml '
   {
     "apiVersion": .apiVersion,
     "kind": .kind,
     "data": .data,
     "metadata": {"name": .metadata.name},
     "type": .type
   }
   ' > ~/crunchy-source-replication-cert.yaml
   ```

## Deploy Percona Operator for PostgreSQL and PostgreSQL cluster in standby mode

1. Deploy Percona Operator for PostgreSQL:

   ```
   kubectl apply --server-side -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/percona/percona-postgresql-operator/v3.1.0/deploy/bundle.yaml -n ${
   ```

1. Import the TLS Secrets using the configuration files you created earlier:

   ```
   kubectl apply -f ~/crunchy-source-cluster-cert.yaml -n ${
   kubectl apply -f ~/crunchy-source-replication-cert.yaml -n $NAMESPACE
   ```

1. Create the shared Secret for the backup storage. You can reuse the same Secret configuration file from the [Adapt the configuration for Crunchy PostgreSQL cluster](#adapt-the-configuration-for-crunchy-postgresql-cluster) step:

   ```
   echo "apiVersion: v1   
   kind: Secret
   metadata:
     name: percona-pgbackrest-secret
   stringData:
     s3.conf: |
       [global]
       repo1-s3-key=<your-access-key>
       repo1-s3-key-secret=<your-access-secret>
   " | kubectl apply -n $NAMESPACE -f -
   ```

1. Edit the `deploy/cr.yaml` and specify the following configuration:

   - For the standby cluster:

     - Set `standby.enabled` to `true`.
     - Specify the repository name to restore from in the `standby.repoName` option.
     - Specify the name of the service of the Crunchy PostgreSQL to stream data from. The Service name follows the pattern `<service-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`.
     - Specify the port of this service.

     Replace example names such as `crunchy-source-ha`, `crunchy-source-pgbackrest`, and `cluster1-pgbouncer` if you use different cluster names. The service name `crunchy-source-ha` in the following example is derived from the source `PostgresCluster` name `crunchy-source`. Replace `<CRUNCHY_NS>` with the namespace of the Crunchy cluster.

     ```
     spec:
        standby:
          enabled: true                     
          host: crunchy-source-ha.<CRUNCHY_NS>.svc.cluster.local
          port: 5432
          repoName: repo1
     ```

   - For the mutual TLS communication, reference the TLS Secrets you created for the `secrets.customTLSSecret` and `secrets.customReplicationTLSSecret` options

     ```
     secrets:
       customTLSSecret:
         name: crunchy-source-cluster-cert 
       customReplicationTLSSecret:
         name: crunchy-source-replication-cert
     ```

     pgBouncer doesn’t work while the cluster uses the Crunchy certificates

     The Crunchy server certificate is issued only for the `crunchy-source-primary` and `crunchy-source-replicas` host names. With this certificate, Percona pgBouncer service `cluster1-pgbouncer` can’t connect to PostgreSQL, and clients that connect to `cluster1-primary` with `sslmode=verify-full` fail on the host name check. The Operator also doesn’t renew these certificates. They expire one year after Crunchy issued them.

     Keep these certificates only for the migration. After the cutover, [switch the cluster to Operator-managed certificates](#switch-to-operator-managed-tls-certificates).

   - Configure the backup storage to exactly match the configuration on the Crunchy PostgreSQL cluster:

   ```
   backups:
       pgbackrest:
       ....
         configuration:
           - secret:
               name: percona-pgbackrest-secret
         global:
           # Must match repo1-path in the Crunchy source cluster exactly.
           repo1-path: /crunchy-to-percona/repo1
           repo1-s3-uri-style: path
           repo1-s3-verify-tls: "n" # Skip for AWS S3
         repos:
           - name: repo1
             s3:
               bucket: <YOUR-BUCKET-HERE>
               endpoint: s3.amazonaws.com
               region: <YOUR-REGION-HERE>
    #The rest of your configuration
   ```

   - If the Crunchy cluster uses tablespace volumes (`spec.instances[].tablespaceVolumes`), add a `tablespaceVolumes` entry with **the same name** for each tablespace to the Percona instance, for example `tablespaceVolumes: [{name: ts1, dataVolumeClaimSpec: {accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce], resources: {requests: {storage: 5Gi}}}}]`. Without it, the standby can’t create the tablespace directories and doesn’t start.

1. Create the Percona PostgreSQL cluster

   ```
   kubectl apply -f deploy/cr.yaml -n $NAMESPACE
   ```

   The Percona Operator deploys the cluster and:

   - Restores the base backup from the S3 bucket.
   - Replays WAL from S3 until it catches up with the live Crunchy cluster.
   - Switches to streaming replication from `crunchy-source-ha`.

1. Wait for the cluster to report the `Ready` status:

   ```
   kubectl wait perconapgcluster/cluster1 \
     -n $NAMESPACE \
     --for=jsonpath='{.status.state}'=ready \
     --timeout=600s
   ```

   Expected output

   ```
   perconapgcluster.pgv2.percona.com/cluster1 condition met
   ```

1. Verify the data is replicated on the standby.

   - Export the standby leader Pod as an environment variable. The standby leader replicates from Crunchy, and the other Pods replicate from it. The Operator labels the standby leader with `role=primary`:

   ```
   STANDBY_POD=$(kubectl get pod -n $NAMESPACE \
   -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=cluster1,postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/role=primary \
   -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
   ```

   - Connect to the pod and verify the cluster is replicating:

   ```
   kubectl -n "${NAMESPACE}" exec "${STANDBY_POD}" -c database -- \
   psql -t -c "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery(), pg_last_wal_replay_lsn();"
   ```

   You should see `t` for `pg_is_in_recovery()` and a non-null LSN.

   Sample output

   ```
   t                 | 0/14000000
   ```

## Verify streaming replication lag before cutover

On the Crunchy **primary** Pod, confirm the Percona standby is connected and lag is acceptable:

1. Identify the primary:

   ```
   CRUNCHY_PRIMARY=$(kubectl get pod \
   -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=crunchy-source,postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/role=master \
     -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
   ```

1. Exec to the primary and verify the replication lag:

   ```
   kubectl -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" exec "${CRUNCHY_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     psql -c "
       SELECT application_name, client_addr, state,
              pg_wal_lsn_diff(sent_lsn, replay_lsn) AS byte_lag,
              write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag
       FROM pg_stat_replication;
     "
   ```

   The output also lists the Crunchy replicas. The Percona standby leader is the row whose `application_name` starts with `cluster1-instance1`.

   Sample output

   ```
      application_name         | client_addr |   state   | byte_lag |    write_lag    |    flush_lag    |   replay_lag
   ----------------------------+-------------+-----------+----------+-----------------+-----------------+-----------------
    crunchy-source-instance1-n642-0 | 10.76.0.6   | streaming |        0 | 00:00:00.004238 | 00:00:00.00733  | 00:00:00.009044
    crunchy-source-instance1-shr4-0 | 10.76.2.9   | streaming |        0 | 00:00:00.011289 | 00:00:00.013495 | 00:00:00.014209
    cluster1-instance1-lfnc-0       | 10.76.2.11  | streaming |        0 | 00:00:00.001273 | 00:00:00.002045 | 00:00:00.002287
   (3 rows)
   ```

Proceed only when `write_lag` and `replay_lag` are null or within your policy (for example a few seconds).

## Cut over the Crunchy PostgreSQL cluster

Now you are ready for the cutover. Note that this step causes downtime as both clusters will be in standby mode and will not accept writes.

1. Patch the Crunchy PostgreSQL cluster to the standby mode. Patroni shuts down the primary cleanly, which archives its last WAL segment to the shared repository. The `repoName` option makes Crunchy a standby that follows this repository, which is what [Rollback](#rollback) relies on:

   ```
   kubectl patch postgrescluster crunchy-source \
     -n $CRUNCHY_NS \
     --type=merge \
     -p '{"spec": {"standby": {"enabled": true, "repoName": "repo1"}}}'
   ```

1. Wait until the former primary reports recovery. Right after the patch, the check can still return `f` or a connection error for a few seconds while Patroni restarts PostgreSQL:

   ```
   until [ "$(kubectl -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" exec "${CRUNCHY_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     psql -tAc 'SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();' 2>/dev/null)" = "t" ]; do
     echo "Waiting for ${CRUNCHY_PRIMARY} to enter recovery..."
     sleep 2
   done
   echo "${CRUNCHY_PRIMARY} is in recovery"
   ```

## (Optional) Shut down the Crunchy cluster

After the Percona standby has replayed WAL, shut down Crunchy to avoid split-brain:

```
kubectl patch postgrescluster crunchy-source \
  -n $CRUNCHY_NS \
  --type=merge \
  -p '{"spec": {"shutdown": true}}'
```

## Promote Percona PostgreSQL cluster

Before promoting the Percona PostgreSQL cluster, make sure it has finished replaying all WAL (Write-Ahead Log) data.

After the Crunchy cluster is shut down, no new WAL files will be generated. The Percona standby will keep replaying existing WAL files from S3 object storage, and its Log Sequence Number (LSN) will advance each time new WAL is applied.

Once the LSN value stops changing and stays the same across two consecutive checks, it means all available WAL has been replayed and it’s safe to promote the standby cluster to be the new primary.

1. Verify the Percona standby cluster has stopped replaying WAL files. The Operator can restart the standby Pods after you created the cluster, so look up the standby leader again first:

   ```
   STANDBY_POD=$(kubectl get pod -n $NAMESPACE \
     -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=cluster1,postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/role=primary \
     -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
   ```

   Then check the replay position:

   ```
   kubectl -n $NAMESPACE exec "${STANDBY_POD}" -c database -- \
     psql -t -c "SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn();"
   ```

   Repeat this command several times until the LSN value stops advancing.

1. Promote the Percona PostgreSQL cluster to be the new primary by patching the cluster:

   ```
   kubectl patch perconapgcluster cluster1 \
     -n $NAMESPACE \
     --type=merge \
     -p '{"spec": {"standby": {"enabled": false}}}'
   ```

1. Wait until the cluster leaves recovery mode and accepts writes. Don’t rely on the cluster `ready` status for this: it stays `ready` during the promotion, so `kubectl wait` for this status returns immediately.

   - Identify the primary Pod:

   ```
   PERCONA_PRIMARY=$(kubectl get pod -n $NAMESPACE \
    -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=cluster1,postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/role=primary \
    -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
   ```

   - Check the recovery mode until the Pod reports `f`, which means the instance is read-write:

   ```
   until [ "$(kubectl -n "${NAMESPACE}" exec "${PERCONA_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     psql -tAc 'SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();' 2>/dev/null)" = "f" ]; do
     echo "Waiting for ${PERCONA_PRIMARY} to accept writes..."
     sleep 2
   done
   echo "${PERCONA_PRIMARY} accepts writes"
   ```

   The promotion usually takes a few seconds.

1. After promoting the Percona cluster, it is important to confirm that the `pgBackRest` stanza has been created. The stanza is required for managing backups and enabling restores. Without it, regular backup operations and recovery from backup will not be possible. Waiting for `stanzaCreated` to become `true` ensures that backup tooling has been initialized properly before proceeding.

   ```
   kubectl wait perconapgcluster/cluster1 \
     -n $NAMESPACE \
     --for=jsonpath='{.status.pgbackrest.repos[0].stanzaCreated}'=true \
     --timeout=300s
   ```

   Expected output

   ```
   perconapgcluster.pgv2.percona.com/cluster1 condition met
   ```

## Take a post-migration backup

After the promotion, `cluster1` still archives WAL to the repository path it shares with Crunchy, and the Operator has already taken an incremental backup there on top of Crunchy’s full backup. Move `cluster1` to its own repository path and take a full backup there. This gives the Percona cluster backups that don’t depend on the Crunchy archive.

This step ends the rollback window

After you change the repository path, Crunchy no longer receives the WAL from `cluster1`. If you roll back after this point, Crunchy doesn’t get the writes made on `cluster1`. Do this step only when you no longer need [Rollback](#rollback). Until then, `cluster1` can keep using the shared path.

Do this step before you point applications to `cluster1`. The WAL that `cluster1` generates between the path change and the stanza creation isn’t stored in either repository.

1. Change the repository path. Use a path that no other cluster uses:

   ```
   kubectl patch perconapgcluster cluster1 \
     -n $NAMESPACE \
     --type=merge \
     -p '{"spec":{"backups":{"pgbackrest":{"global":{"repo1-path":"/percona/cluster1/repo1"}}}}}'
   ```

1. Wait until the `pgBackRest` configuration on the primary Pod shows the new path:

   ```
   until kubectl -n "${NAMESPACE}" exec "${PERCONA_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     grep -qE 'repo1-path *= */percona/cluster1/repo1$' /etc/pgbackrest/conf.d/pgbackrest_instance.conf 2>/dev/null; do
     echo "Waiting for the new repository path..."
     sleep 5
   done
   ```

1. Create the `pgBackRest` stanza in the new path. The Operator doesn’t do it when only the path changes:

   ```
   kubectl -n "${NAMESPACE}" exec "${PERCONA_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     pgbackrest --stanza=db stanza-create
   ```

   Until the stanza exists, WAL archiving to the new path fails. In Operator versions 3.0.0 and 3.1.0, `pg_stat_archiver` doesn’t show these failures, so don’t use it to check archiving.

1. Wait until the repository host Pod also has the new path. Backups run from this Pod, and it gets the new configuration up to a minute later than the primary:

   ```
   until kubectl -n $NAMESPACE exec cluster1-repo-host-0 -c pgbackrest -- \
     grep -qE 'repo1-path *= */percona/cluster1/repo1$' /etc/pgbackrest/conf.d/pgbackrest_repo.conf 2>/dev/null; do
     echo "Waiting for the repository host..."
     sleep 5
   done
   ```

Then take a full backup in the new path:

1. Create the `post-migration-backup.yaml` configuration file. Set `--type=full` in `options`: without it, `pgBackRest` makes an incremental backup on top of the last full backup in the repository.

   post-migration-backup.yaml

   ```
   apiVersion: pgv2.percona.com/v2
   kind: PerconaPGBackup
   metadata:
     name: post-migration-backup
   spec:
     pgCluster: cluster1
     repoName: repo1
     options:
       - --type=full
   ```

1. Apply the configuration to start the backup:

   ```
   kubectl apply -f post-migration-backup.yaml -n $NAMESPACE
   ```

1. Wait for the backup job to complete:

   ```
   kubectl wait perconapgbackup/post-migration-backup \
     -n $NAMESPACE \
     --for=jsonpath='{.status.state}'=Succeeded \
     --timeout=600s
   ```

   Expected output

   ```
   perconapgbackup.pgv2.percona.com/post-migration-backup condition met
   ```

1. Check that the backup is a full backup:

   ```
   kubectl get perconapgbackup post-migration-backup \
     -n $NAMESPACE \
     -o jsonpath='{.status.backupType}{"\n"}'
   ```

   The output is `full`.

## Switch to Operator-managed TLS certificates

The cluster still uses the TLS certificates imported from Crunchy. They don’t cover the `cluster1` host names, so `cluster1-pgbouncer` can’t connect to PostgreSQL, and the Operator doesn’t renew them. Replace them with certificates that the Operator issues and renews.

Like the repository path change, this step ends the rollback window: replication between the clusters relies on the Crunchy certificates.

1. Remove the references to the Crunchy certificates from the cluster configuration:

   ```
   kubectl patch perconapgcluster cluster1 \
     -n $NAMESPACE \
     --type=json \
     -p='[
       {"op":"remove","path":"/spec/secrets/customTLSSecret"},
       {"op":"remove","path":"/spec/secrets/customReplicationTLSSecret"}
     ]'
   ```

   The Operator creates the `cluster1-cluster-cert` and `cluster1-replication-cert` Secrets, restarts the pgBouncer Pods and then restarts the PostgreSQL Pods one by one.

1. Watch the PostgreSQL Pods:

   ```
   kubectl get pod -n $NAMESPACE -w \
     -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=cluster1,postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/data=postgres
   ```

   The restart can stop after the first replica: the restarted replica trusts only the new certificate authority, so it can’t connect to the primary that still uses the Crunchy certificate. The replica stays not ready, and its `database` container log shows `certificate verify failed`. If this happens, finish the switch manually:

   1. Delete the other replica Pod that still runs with the old certificates, so that it restarts with the new ones:

      ```
      kubectl delete pod <old-replica-pod> -n $NAMESPACE
      ```

   1. The replicas with the new certificates can’t stream from the primary, so they replay WAL only from the backup repository and lag behind. Patroni refuses a switchover to a lagging replica. Make the primary archive its current WAL file, then check that the lag of the replica you switch to is `0`:

      ```
      kubectl -n "${NAMESPACE}" exec "${PERCONA_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
        psql -c "SELECT pg_switch_wal();"
      kubectl -n "${NAMESPACE}" exec "${PERCONA_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
        patronictl list
      ```

      Repeat `patronictl list` until the replay lag of the replica (the last `Lag` column) shows `0`. The first `Lag` column can keep growing: the replica doesn’t stream from the primary, so its received position doesn’t move.

   1. Make the replica that runs with the new certificates the primary. Writes stop for about 10 seconds during the switchover:

      ```
      kubectl -n "${NAMESPACE}" exec "${PERCONA_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
        patronictl switchover --candidate <new-replica-pod> --force
      ```

      Check the output for `Successfully switched over`. The command exits with code `0` even when the switchover fails, for example with `Switchover failed, details: 503`. In this case, repeat the previous step and try again.

      The Operator then restarts the former primary with the new certificates.

1. After all PostgreSQL Pods are restarted and ready, check that the cluster reports the `ready` state:

   ```
   kubectl get perconapgcluster cluster1 -n $NAMESPACE
   ```

1. Check that clients can connect with full certificate verification. Save the certificate authority of the cluster to a file:

   ```
   kubectl get secret cluster1-cluster-cert -n $NAMESPACE \
     -o jsonpath='{.data.ca\.crt}' | base64 --decode > cluster1-ca.crt
   ```

   Use this file as `sslrootcert` with `sslmode=verify-full` when you connect to `cluster1-primary` or `cluster1-pgbouncer`. Applications that trusted the Crunchy certificate authority must use this one instead.

## Update the application connection string

After you migrated to Percona Operator for PostgreSQL, update your application connection string to use the new Percona cluster. If you must send traffic to `cluster1` before you [switch the TLS certificates](#switch-to-operator-managed-tls-certificates), use the `cluster1-primary` Service with `sslmode=require` instead of pgBouncer.

1. Get the `pgBouncer` service exposed by the Percona Operator:

   ```
   kubectl get service -n $NAMESPACE cluster1-pgbouncer
   ```

The output will show the `cluster1-pgbouncer` service, along with its ClusterIP and port.

1. Update your application’s connection string to use the `pgBouncer` service name (from the previous step) as the PostgreSQL host. For example:

   ```
   Host:   cluster1-pgbouncer.$NAMESPACE.svc.cluster.local
   Port:   5432
   ```

Replace `${NAMESPACE}` with your cluster’s namespace. Update your application configuration to point to this service, ensuring it now connects to your Percona Operator for PostgreSQL deployment.

## Rollback

The standby path is the most rollback-friendly of the [migration options](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/migrate-from-crunchy.html): Crunchy and Percona share the same `pgBackRest` repository until you move `cluster1` to its own repository path.

### Before you move cluster1 to its own repository

You can return write traffic to Crunchy while `cluster1` still archives WAL to the shared repository and uses the Crunchy certificates. In other words, before you complete [Take a post-migration backup](#take-a-post-migration-backup) and [Switch to Operator-managed TLS certificates](#switch-to-operator-managed-tls-certificates). The Crunchy `PostgresCluster` must still exist.

**What happens to the writes made on `cluster1` after the promotion:**

- If the WAL of `cluster1` reaches the shared repository before Crunchy is promoted, Crunchy replays it, and these writes are on Crunchy after the rollback. This is the normal case when you follow the steps below and WAL archiving works. Don’t copy these writes to Crunchy manually: you would duplicate them.
- If some of this WAL is missing from the repository, for example, because archiving failed or `cluster1` stopped without a clean shutdown, the writes in it are lost. Crunchy can then reuse sequence values that `cluster1` already used, and `cluster1` ends up on a timeline that diverged from Crunchy. In this case, delete `cluster1` and create it again as a standby.

To roll back, do the following:

1. Stop application writes to `cluster1`.

1. Record the position of the last write on `cluster1` and the WAL file that contains it, and make `cluster1` archive this file. You need these values to check that Crunchy gets every write. Run this and the following steps in the same terminal session, so that the `FINAL_LSN` and `FINAL_WAL` variables are kept, or note the values from the output:

   ```
   PERCONA_PRIMARY=$(kubectl get pod -n "${NAMESPACE}" \
     -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=cluster1,postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/role=primary \
     -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
   FINAL_LSN=$(kubectl -n "${NAMESPACE}" exec "${PERCONA_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     psql -tAc "SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();")
   FINAL_WAL=$(kubectl -n "${NAMESPACE}" exec "${PERCONA_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     psql -tAc "SELECT pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn());")
   kubectl -n "${NAMESPACE}" exec "${PERCONA_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     psql -tAc "SELECT pg_switch_wal();" >/dev/null
   echo "Final LSN: ${FINAL_LSN}, WAL file: ${FINAL_WAL}"
   ```

1. Put `cluster1` back into standby so it stops acting as the primary (Patroni will follow the Custom Resource). The `standby.host`, `standby.port`, and `standby.repoName` you configured earlier should still be present; merge only toggles standby on:

   ```
   kubectl patch perconapgcluster cluster1 \
     -n $NAMESPACE \
     --type=merge \
     -p '{"spec": {"standby": {"enabled": true, "repoName": "repo1"}}}'
   ```

1. Wait until every `cluster1` Pod is in recovery. A single check right after the patch isn’t enough: the primary keeps returning `f`, and then a connection error, for a few seconds while Patroni demotes it.

   ```
   for pod in $(kubectl get pod -n "${NAMESPACE}" -o name \
     -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=cluster1,postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/data=postgres); do
     until [ "$(kubectl -n "${NAMESPACE}" exec "${pod}" -c database -- \
       psql -tAc 'SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();' 2>/dev/null)" = "t" ]; do
       echo "Waiting for ${pod} to enter recovery..."
       sleep 2
     done
     echo "${pod} is in recovery"
   done
   ```

   Don’t promote Crunchy while cluster1 is still a primary

   If you take Crunchy out of standby while `cluster1` still accepts writes, both clusters accept writes and archive WAL to the same `pgBackRest` stanza on different timelines. Neither Operator reports an error. When `cluster1` later follows Crunchy again, `pg_rewind` discards the writes made on `cluster1` in the meantime.

1. Check that the WAL file with the last write is in the shared repository. The following command tries to fetch the file from the repository for about 6 minutes:

   ```
   ARCHIVED=no
   for i in $(seq 1 60); do
     if kubectl -n "${NAMESPACE}" exec "${PERCONA_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
       pgbackrest --stanza=db archive-get "${FINAL_WAL}" /tmp/rollback-wal-check >/dev/null 2>&1; then
       ARCHIVED=yes; echo "${FINAL_WAL} is in the repository"; break
     fi
     echo "Waiting for ${FINAL_WAL} to be archived..."
     sleep 5
   done
   kubectl -n "${NAMESPACE}" exec "${PERCONA_PRIMARY}" -c database -- rm -f /tmp/rollback-wal-check
   [ "${ARCHIVED}" = yes ] || echo "ERROR: ${FINAL_WAL} is not in the repository. Don't continue."
   ```

   Continue only if the output ends with `is in the repository`. If it ends with the error, WAL archiving on `cluster1` failed, and the writes in this file and the files before it would be lost after the rollback. Don’t rely on `pg_stat_archiver` to check this: in Operator versions 3.0.0 and 3.1.0 it reports WAL files as archived even when the upload failed.

   Fixing the cause, for example wrong storage credentials, isn’t enough: PostgreSQL doesn’t retry WAL files that the failed archive command reported as archived. After you fix the cause, push the missing WAL files from `cluster1` to the repository manually. The files are still in the `pg_wal` directory of the Pod. Replace `pg18` with your PostgreSQL major version:

   ```
   kubectl -n "${NAMESPACE}" exec "${PERCONA_PRIMARY}" -c database -- bash -c '
     cd /pgdata/pg18/pg_wal
     for f in $(ls | grep -E "^'"${FINAL_WAL:0:8}"'[0-9A-F]{16}$" | sort); do
       [[ "$f" > "'"${FINAL_WAL}"'" ]] && break
       pgbackrest --stanza=db --no-archive-async archive-push "$PWD/$f"
     done'
   ```

   This command pushes every WAL file of the current timeline up to `FINAL_WAL`. Pushing a file that is already in the repository with the same content succeeds, so the command is safe to run. Then repeat this step.

1. If you applied [(Optional) Shut down the Crunchy cluster](#optional-shut-down-the-crunchy-cluster), clear shutdown:

   ```
   kubectl patch postgrescluster crunchy-source \
     -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     --type=merge \
     -p '{"spec": {"shutdown": false}}'
   ```

1. Wait until every Crunchy Pod has replayed WAL up to the last write on `cluster1`. Crunchy is still a standby and replays this WAL from the shared repository. If you promote it before it reaches this position, the remaining writes are lost.

   If you shut down Crunchy, it starts the former primary first and the other instances later. Wait until all instances are ready. Set the number to the `replicas` value of the `instance1` instance set (`3` in this example):

   ```
   kubectl wait postgrescluster.postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/crunchy-source \
     -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     --for=jsonpath='{.status.instances[?(@.name=="instance1")].readyReplicas}'=3 \
     --timeout=600s
   ```

   Then check the replay position on every Crunchy Pod:

   ```
   for pod in $(kubectl get pod -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" -o name \
     -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=crunchy-source,postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/data=postgres); do
     until [ "$(kubectl -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" exec "${pod}" -c database -- \
       psql -tAc "SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= '${FINAL_LSN}'::pg_lsn;" 2>/dev/null)" = "t" ]; do
       echo "Waiting for ${pod} to replay up to ${FINAL_LSN}..."
       sleep 2
     done
     echo "${pod} has replayed up to ${FINAL_LSN}"
   done
   ```

1. Take Crunchy out of standby so Patroni can promote it back to primary:

   ```
   kubectl patch postgrescluster crunchy-source \
     -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     --type=merge \
     -p '{"spec": {"standby": {"enabled": false}}}'
   ```

1. Confirm roles: Crunchy should accept writes and `cluster1` should be in recovery until replication catches up. The `role=master` label appears on the promoted Pod only after the promotion, so wait for it:

   ```
   until CRUNCHY_PRIMARY=$(kubectl get pod \
     -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=crunchy-source,postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/role=master \
     -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}' 2>/dev/null) && [ -n "${CRUNCHY_PRIMARY}" ]; do
     echo "Waiting for the Crunchy primary Pod..."
     sleep 2
   done

   until [ "$(kubectl -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" exec "${CRUNCHY_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     psql -tAc 'SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();' 2>/dev/null)" = "f" ]; do
     echo "Waiting for ${CRUNCHY_PRIMARY} to accept writes..."
     sleep 2
   done
   echo "${CRUNCHY_PRIMARY} accepts writes"
   ```

   Check that `cluster1` follows Crunchy:

   ```
   kubectl -n "${NAMESPACE}" exec "${PERCONA_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     psql -t -c "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();"
   ```

   You should see `t` on Percona while it follows Crunchy.

1. Restore the password of the Crunchy pgBouncer user. After the promotion, the Percona Operator set a new password for the `_crunchypgbouncer` role, and the rollback carried this password back to Crunchy. Until you restore it, the Crunchy pgBouncer fails to authenticate. Set the role password back to the value from the Crunchy pgBouncer Secret:

   ```
   VERIFIER=$(kubectl get secret crunchy-source-pgbouncer -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     -o jsonpath='{.data.pgbouncer-verifier}' | base64 --decode)
   kubectl -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" exec "${CRUNCHY_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     psql -c "ALTER ROLE \"_crunchypgbouncer\" PASSWORD '${VERIFIER}';"
   ```

   pgBouncer keeps rejecting connections for about 30 seconds after the change with `server login has been failing`. This is pgBouncer’s retry delay. Retry the connection after that.

1. Point applications back at the Crunchy `pgBouncer` Service:

   ```
   kubectl get service -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=crunchy-source,postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/role=pgbouncer
   ```

If you migrate to Percona again after a rollback

Step 10 sets the Crunchy password for `_crunchypgbouncer`, and `cluster1` replicates it. After you promote `cluster1` again, the Operator doesn’t reset this password, so `cluster1-pgbouncer` fails to authenticate. After the promotion, set the password from the Percona pgBouncer Secret on the `cluster1` primary:

```
VERIFIER=$(kubectl get secret cluster1-pgbouncer -n "${NAMESPACE}" \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.pgbouncer-verifier}' | base64 --decode)
kubectl -n $NAMESPACE exec "${PERCONA_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
  psql -c "ALTER ROLE \"_crunchypgbouncer\" PASSWORD '${VERIFIER}';"
```

### After you move cluster1 to its own repository

After `cluster1` archives WAL to its own repository path, Crunchy no longer receives its writes. You should treat Crunchy as a historical reference, not a live paired primary.

Rolling back from here is the same idea as a fresh restore: deploy or restore a Crunchy cluster from the repository state you need, or follow [Migrate from Crunchy using backup and restore](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/migrate-from-crunchy-backup-restore.html) in reverse order for your environment. Plan the rollback **before** cutover if you require a guaranteed fast path.

## Troubleshooting

### Percona standby cannot resolve or reach the Crunchy primary

Confirm the PostgreSQL HA Service for `crunchy-source` resolves from the Percona database Pod. Replace `crunchy-source-ha` if your Service name differs.

```
kubectl -n "${NAMESPACE}" exec "${STANDBY_POD}" -c database -- \
  bash -c "getent hosts crunchy-source-ha.${CRUNCHY_NS}.svc.cluster.local"
```

If DNS fails, check Service names and namespaces. If DNS succeeds but TCP fails, check NetworkPolicies, service mesh rules, and firewalls between namespaces.

### Standby fails with `Read-only file system` for `/tablespaces`

The standby leader is in `CrashLoopBackOff`, and its log shows `unable to create path '/tablespaces': [30] Read-only file system` or `pg_basebackup: error: could not create directory "/tablespaces": Read-only file system`, followed by `Failed to bootstrap cluster`. The Crunchy cluster uses tablespace volumes, and the Percona instance has no `tablespaceVolumes` entry with the same name. Add the entries to the cluster configuration.

### Replication authentication errors

The Percona standby connects to Crunchy as the PostgreSQL role `_crunchyrepl` using the replication TLS material. Ensure `crunchy-source-replication-cert` exists in `$NAMESPACE` and matches what Crunchy generated (re-export from `"${CRUNCHY_NS}"` if you rotated certificates).

```
kubectl get secret crunchy-source-replication-cert -n "${NAMESPACE}"
```

Verify the `PerconaPGCluster` still references it under `secrets.customReplicationTLSSecret` and `secrets.customTLSSecret` as in [Deploy Percona Operator for PostgreSQL and PostgreSQL cluster in standby mode](#deploy-percona-operator-for-postgresql-and-postgresql-cluster-in-standby-mode).

### `pgBackRest` restore or WAL archive problems

Symptoms include failed restore Jobs, missing `archive.info`, or the standby never leaving base backup replay.

1. Confirm `repo1-path` is **identical** on Crunchy and on `cluster1` (for example `/crunchy-to-percona/repo1` in this guide). This applies until you [move `cluster1` to its own repository path](#take-a-post-migration-backup). After the move, the paths differ on purpose.

   ```
   kubectl get postgrescluster crunchy-source -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     -o jsonpath='{.spec.backups.pgbackrest.global.repo1-path}{"\n"}'

   kubectl get perconapgcluster cluster1 -n $NAMESPACE \
     -o jsonpath='{.spec.backups.pgbackrest.global.repo1-path}{"\n"}'
   ```

1. Confirm both clusters use credentials that can read and write the same bucket (equivalent Secrets). See [Configure backup storage](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/backups-storage.html) for TLS flags such as `repo1-s3-verify-tls` and path-style settings.

1. From a throwaway Pod in `$NAMESPACE`, verify object storage reachability with your endpoint, bucket, and keys (adapt for your provider):

   ```
   kubectl run s3-check \
     --image=perconalab/awscli \
     --restart=Never \
     -n $NAMESPACE \
     -- bash -c "
       AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID='<your-access-key>' \
       AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY='<your-secret-key>' \
       AWS_DEFAULT_REGION='<your-region>' \
       aws --endpoint-url 'https://<your-s3-endpoint>' \
           --no-verify-ssl \
           s3 ls s3://<your-bucket>
     "
   ```

   The command finishes quickly, so read its output from the Pod logs, and then delete the Pod:

   ```
   kubectl wait pod/s3-check -n $NAMESPACE \
     --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded --timeout=120s
   kubectl logs s3-check -n $NAMESPACE
   kubectl delete pod s3-check -n $NAMESPACE
   ```

### Timeline history file missing after promotion (Crunchy archive)

Some Crunchy PGO configurations using async archive mode can hit a missing timeline history file on the archive after promotion (see [Crunchy PGO issue #4472](https://github.com/CrunchyData/postgres-operator/issues/4472) ). If `pgBackRest` or replicas complain about `*.history` on the archive, push the file once from the **new** primary:

```
kubectl -n "${NAMESPACE}" exec "${PERCONA_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
  bash -c "
    pgbackrest --stanza=db --no-archive-async \
      archive-push \"\${PGDATA}/pg_wal/00000002.history\" || true
  "
```

Adjust the filename to match the timeline file reported in your logs.

# Migrate from Crunchy to Percona Operator for PostgreSQL using backup and restore

You can migrate by taking a full `pgBackRest` backup on your Crunchy `PostgresCluster` and creating a new `PerconaPGCluster` that restores from that backup before its first start. This path is straightforward when you can accept downtime between the final backup and an application cutover.

| Benefits                                                                                                                                                                                            | Trade-offs                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| - A clear cutover point - Room to rehearse restore and validation before switching applications - The option to roll back to Crunchy until you decommission the source cluster and redirect traffic | - Writes stop from the cutover until the Percona cluster is ready. - Downtime spans the restore and validation time. The restore replays the WAL archived after the migration backup, so a recent backup shortens it. |

For **near-zero downtime**, use [Migrate from Crunchy using a standby cluster](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/migrate-from-crunchy-standby.html) instead.

## Versions used in this guide

For this migration tutorial, we use the following versions of the Operators:

- Crunchy PostgreSQL Operator 5.8.x
- Percona Operator for PostgreSQL 3.x.x
- An AWS S3 storage for backups. If you use another remote storage, configure access to it for both clusters.

## Before you migrate

Complete the [Pre-migration compatibility checks](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/migrate-checklist.html). Physical methods require a matching PostgreSQL major version and CPU architecture.

## Prerequisites

Ensure you have the following:

- A Kubernetes cluster running on one of the [supported platforms](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/System-Requirements.html#supported-platforms) with permissions to create namespaces, CRDs, Roles, and Deployments.
- [Helm](https://helm.sh/) 3.x (if you install operators or optional in-cluster object storage with Helm).
- `kubectl` or `oc`.
- [yq](https://github.com/mikefarah/yq) YAML processor (optional, for manifest tricks used in other migration guides).
- A remote backup storage reachable from Pods in both the Crunchy and Percona namespaces.

## Before you start

1. Create or choose namespaces for Crunchy and Percona and export them.

   ```
   export CRUNCHY_NS=postgres-operator
   export NAMESPACE=pgo
   kubectl create namespace postgres-operator
   kubectl create namespace pgo
   ```

1. Clone the Percona Operator repository at the release you will deploy so you can base your `PerconaPGCluster` manifest on the default `deploy/cr.yaml`:

   ```
   git clone -b v3.1.0 https://github.com/percona/percona-postgresql-operator
   ```

## Configure Crunchy PostgreSQL cluster for remote backups

If you already run Crunchy PGO, configure the `PostgresCluster` object so that `pgBackRest` writes backups and WAL (Write-Ahead Logs) to remote storage that the Percona cluster can access and read. This ensures that Percona can restore from your latest backups when you perform the migration.

If you are deploying Crunchy for testing or migration rehearsal, make sure your `PostgresCluster` manifest configures `pgBackRest` to use the same remote object storage (for example, S3 or S3-compatible, Google Cloud Storage, or compatible endpoint) for both backups and WAL archives. The Percona PostgreSQL cluster will need access to this storage location for a successful restore.

This involves:

- Creating a Secret with the required credentials for your object storage (e.g., S3 access keys or GCS service account).
- Referencing that Secret under the `spec.backups.pgbackrest.configuration` section in your Crunchy `PostgresCluster` manifest.
- Adding an object storage repository under `spec.backups.pgbackrest.repos` with the bucket, region, endpoint, and other storage details. Note its path: you need it on the Percona side under `spec.dataSource.pgbackrest`. If you don’t set `repo<N>-path`, Crunchy uses `/pgbackrest/repo<N>`, for example, `/pgbackrest/repo2`.
- Adding the `spec.backups.pgbackrest.manual` section, so that you can start a backup to this repository on demand.
- Ensuring network access between Crunchy and Percona namespaces to the object storage endpoint.

See the [standby migration guide](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/migrate-from-crunchy-standby.html#adapt-the-configuration-for-crunchy-postgresql-cluster) for an example manifest that creates the required Secret and configures remote backups and WAL archiving.

### Clusters that already have a backup repository

Many existing Crunchy clusters use a volume (PVC) repository as `repo1`, and keep backups in object storage in `repo2` or a higher-numbered repository. Check which repositories your cluster has:

```
kubectl get postgrescluster.postgres-operator.crunchydata.com crunchy-source \
  -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
  -o jsonpath='{range .spec.backups.pgbackrest.repos[*]}{.name}{"\t"}{.s3.bucket}{.gcs.bucket}{.azure.container}{.volume.volumeClaimSpec.resources.requests.storage}{"\n"}{end}'
```

Sample output

```
repo1   2Gi
repo2   my-backup-bucket
```

A bucket or container name means an object storage repository. A storage size means a volume repository. In this example, `repo1` is a volume repository and `repo2` is in object storage.

- If the cluster already has an object storage repository, use it for the migration. You don’t need to rename it to `repo1`.
- If the cluster only has a volume repository, add an object storage repository with the next free name, for example, `repo2`. Don’t replace or remove `repo1`. The Percona cluster can’t restore from a volume repository of another cluster: neither `dataSource.pgbackrest` with a `volume` repository nor `dataSource.postgresCluster` can read it.

Changing `spec.backups` on an existing Crunchy cluster restarts its PostgreSQL Pods. Plan this change for a maintenance window.

The rest of this guide uses `repo1` in object storage. If your repository has a different name, set `manual.repoName` to it, use it in the `stanzaCreated` wait command, and see [how to reference it on the Percona side](#create-the-percona-postgresql-cluster-from-the-crunchy-backup).

Here’s the example configuration of the Crunchy `PostgresCluster` object:

postgres.yaml

```
apiVersion: postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/v1beta1
kind: PostgresCluster
metadata:
  name: crunchy-source
spec:
  postgresVersion: 18
  instances:
    - name: instance1
      replicas: 3
      dataVolumeClaimSpec:
        accessModes:
          - ReadWriteOnce
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 10Gi
  backups:
    pgbackrest:
      configuration:
        - secret:
            name: crunchy-pgbackrest-secret
      manual:
        repoName: repo1
        options:
          - --type=full
      global:
        repo1-path: /crunchy-to-percona/repo1
        repo1-s3-uri-style: path
        repo1-s3-verify-tls: "n"
      repos:
        - name: repo1
          s3:
            bucket: <YOUR-BUCKET-HERE>
            endpoint: s3.amazonaws.com
            region: <YOUR-REGION-HERE>
  proxy:
    pgBouncer:
      replicas: 1
```

Apply the configuration to create a new or update an existing cluster:

```
kubectl apply -f postgres.yaml -n $CRUNCHY_NS
```

Wait until all PostgreSQL instances of the cluster are ready. Set the number to the `replicas` value of the `instance1` instance set (`3` in this example):

```
kubectl wait postgrescluster.postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/crunchy-source \
  -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
  --for=jsonpath='{.status.instances[?(@.name=="instance1")].readyReplicas}'=3 \
  --timeout=600s
```

Expected output

```
postgrescluster.postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/crunchy-source condition met
```

This command waits on the cluster status, so you can run it right after `kubectl apply`. A `kubectl wait pod` command fails with `no matching resources found` if the Pods don’t exist yet.

Wait for the `pgBackRest` stanza to be created. The stanza initializes the backup and restore infrastructure for further backup or restore operations. Specify the repository that stores backups in the object storage (`repo1` in this example):

```
kubectl wait postgrescluster.postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/crunchy-source \
  -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
  --for=jsonpath='{.status.pgbackrest.repos[?(@.name=="repo1")].stanzaCreated}'=true \
  --timeout=300s
```

Expected output

```
postgrescluster.postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/crunchy-source condition met
```

The `stanzaCreated` status confirms that `pgBackRest` has scanned the configuration and the data directory and is ready to manage backups for your cluster.

## Create the migration backup

Add a few test records to your database, then trigger a full backup.

This backup is the starting point for the restore of `cluster1` on Percona. You don’t need to stop application writes for it: the restore replays the WAL that Crunchy archives after the backup. You stop writes later, at the [cutover](#prepare-the-cutover).

1. Identify the primary Pod of the Crunchy PostgreSQL cluster and export it as an environment variable:

   ```
   CRUNCHY_PRIMARY=$(kubectl get pod \
       -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=crunchy-source,postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/role=master \
       -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
       -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
   ```

1. Connect to the Crunchy PostgreSQL cluster and insert some sample data. Use the following command to exec to the primary Pod, create a database and a table and insert some data to it:

   ```
   kubectl exec -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" "${CRUNCHY_PRIMARY}" -c database -- bash -c "
       psql -c 'CREATE DATABASE migrationtest;'
       psql -d migrationtest -c 'CREATE TABLE migration_data (id int PRIMARY KEY, value text);'
       psql -d migrationtest -c \"INSERT INTO migration_data VALUES (1, 'initial-data-before-migration');\"
     "
   ```

1. Start a full backup. The annotation value identifies this backup request, so save it in a variable:

   ```
   BACKUP_ID=$(date +%s)
   kubectl annotate postgrescluster.postgres-operator.crunchydata.com crunchy-source \
     -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     --overwrite \
     postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/pgbackrest-backup="${BACKUP_ID}"
   ```

   The `--overwrite` flag lets you re-run the command if the cluster already has this annotation from an earlier backup.

1. Wait until the Crunchy Operator picks up this backup request:

   ```
   kubectl wait postgrescluster.postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/crunchy-source \
     -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     --for=jsonpath='{.status.pgbackrest.manualBackup.id}'="${BACKUP_ID}" \
     --timeout=120s
   ```

1. Wait for the backup to finish:

   ```
   kubectl wait postgrescluster.postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/crunchy-source \
     -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     --for=jsonpath='{.status.pgbackrest.manualBackup.finished}'=true \
     --timeout=600s
   ```

   On a newly created Crunchy cluster, the Crunchy Operator first completes its automatic initial backup and starts your backup only after that. The timeout covers both backups. For a large cluster, increase it.

   Expected output

   ```
   postgrescluster.postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/crunchy-source condition met
   ```

1. Check that the backup succeeded:

   ```
   kubectl get postgrescluster.postgres-operator.crunchydata.com crunchy-source \
     -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     -o jsonpath='{.status.pgbackrest.manualBackup.succeeded}{"\n"}'
   ```

   The output is `1` for a successful backup.

   If the backup fails, the Crunchy Operator retries it. During the retries, `finished` stays `false` and the previous wait times out, while `status.pgbackrest.manualBackup.failed` counts the failed attempts. Check it with:

   ```
   kubectl get postgrescluster.postgres-operator.crunchydata.com crunchy-source \
     -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     -o jsonpath='{.status.pgbackrest.manualBackup}{"\n"}'
   ```

   To find the backup Job and check its logs, run:

   ```
   kubectl get job -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" \
     -l postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=crunchy-source,postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/pgbackrest-backup=manual
   ```

   After you fix the cause, start the backup again with a new `BACKUP_ID` value.

## Prepare pgBackRest credentials in the Percona namespace

Create a Secret in `$NAMESPACE` with the **same** credentials and storage information such as endpoint and region that you used to configure `pgBackRest` in the Crunchy PostgreSQL cluster.

The following example command creates a Secret with the name `percona-pgbackrest-secret` for the Percona cluster; keep that name if you copy the manifest below.

```
kubectl apply -n "$NAMESPACE" -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: percona-pgbackrest-secret
stringData:
  s3.conf: |
    [global]
    repo1-s3-key=<your-access-key>
    repo1-s3-key-secret=<your-access-secret>
EOF
```

If you use different Secret names, use your name consistently in `spec.dataSource.pgbackrest.configuration` and `spec.backups.pgbackrest.configuration` on `PerconaPGCluster` `cluster1`.

## Deploy Percona Operator for PostgreSQL

1. Deploy Percona Operator for PostgreSQL:

   ```
   kubectl apply --server-side -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/percona/percona-postgresql-operator/v3.1.0/deploy/bundle.yaml -n $NAMESPACE
   ```

1. Wait for the Percona Operator Deployment to become available:

   ```
   kubectl wait deployment percona-postgresql-operator \
     -n "${NAMESPACE}" \
     --for=condition=Available \
     --timeout=120s
   ```

   Expected output

   ```
   deployment.apps/percona-postgresql-operator condition met
   ```

## Prepare the cutover

The Percona cluster restores the migration backup and then replays the WAL that Crunchy archived after it. Writes are carried over up to the last archived WAL file. Crunchy archives the current WAL file when it is full or after `archive_timeout` (60 seconds by default), so the last writes can still be in a WAL file that isn’t archived yet. To carry over every write, make Crunchy archive the current WAL file after you stop writes:

1. Stop application writes to the Crunchy cluster. This is the start of the downtime.

1. Switch to a new WAL file, so that Crunchy archives the current one. Save the name of the archived file:

   ```
   WAL_FILE=$(kubectl -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" exec "${CRUNCHY_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     psql -tAc "SELECT pg_walfile_name(pg_switch_wal());")
   echo "${WAL_FILE}"
   ```

1. Wait until Crunchy reports this file as archived:

   ```
   until [ "$(kubectl -n "${CRUNCHY_NS}" exec "${CRUNCHY_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
     psql -tAc "SELECT last_archived_wal >= '${WAL_FILE}' FROM pg_stat_archiver;")" = "t" ]; do
     echo "Waiting for ${WAL_FILE} to be archived..."
     sleep 2
   done
   ```

Now the repository contains every write. Create the Percona cluster in the next section. You don’t need a new backup.

Restore up to a specific point in time instead

To restore only up to a specific moment, for example, if you can’t stop writes, add point-in-time recovery options to `spec.dataSource.pgbackrest`:

```
dataSource:
  pgbackrest:
    options:
      - --type=time
      - --target="2026-10-15 10:05:55+00"
```

PostgreSQL compares the target with the **commit** time of each transaction. A transaction that commits after the target isn’t restored, even if your application recorded an earlier timestamp for it. Set the target to the commit time of the last transaction you need, or later. You don’t need to add `--target-action=promote`: the Operator adds it.

## Create the Percona PostgreSQL cluster from the Crunchy backup

1. Edit the `deploy/cr.yaml` manifest and specify the following:

   1. Set `spec.postgresVersion` to the same major version as `crunchy-source`.

   1. The `spec.dataSource.pgbackrest` configuration to reference the Secret with the credentials to the object store and to point at the **same** repository path and object store settings as the Crunchy repository you back up to. See [Clone from S3 storage](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/backups-clone.html#clone-from-s3-storage) for these options.

      The repository name in `repo.name` and the `repo<N>-` prefix of the options in `global` and in the Secret must match each other. They don’t need to match the repository name on Crunchy. For example, to restore from a Crunchy `repo2` with the default path, either use `repo2` everywhere (`repo.name: repo2`, `repo2-path: /pgbackrest/repo2`, and `repo2-s3-key` in the Secret), or use `repo1` everywhere and set `repo1-path: /pgbackrest/repo2`. See [Match the repository number](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/backups-clone.html#match-the-repository-number) for details.

   1. Under `spec.backups.pgbackrest`, use a **different** `repo<N>-path` than the Crunchy cluster so new backups do not overwrite the migration archive.

   1. Set the storage size in `spec.instances[].dataVolumeClaimSpec` so that it fits the Crunchy data and WAL. The default `deploy/cr.yaml` requests only 1Gi.

   1. If the Crunchy cluster uses tablespace volumes (`spec.instances[].tablespaceVolumes`), add a `tablespaceVolumes` entry with **the same name** for each tablespace to the Percona instance. The restore writes each tablespace to its original location under `/tablespaces/<name>`, where the Operator mounts the tablespace volume, so the volume must exist. For example:

      ```
      instances:
        - name: instance1
          tablespaceVolumes:
            - name: ts1
              dataVolumeClaimSpec:
                accessModes:
                  - ReadWriteOnce
                resources:
                  requests:
                    storage: 5Gi
      ```

      To store the tablespaces on the data volume instead, add `--tablespace-map-all=/pgdata/tablespaces` to `spec.dataSource.pgbackrest.options`. The tablespace locations then change to `/pgdata/tablespaces/<name>`.

   The following fragment shows the important pieces; merge them with the rest of `deploy/cr.yaml` (images, users, resources) for your environment:

   ```
   metadata:
     name: cluster1
   spec:
     ....
     dataSource:
       pgbackrest:
         stanza: db
         configuration:
           - secret:
               name: percona-pgbackrest-secret
         global:
           # The path of the Crunchy repository: its repo<N>-path value, or /pgbackrest/repo<N> if it isn't set
           repo1-path: /crunchy-to-percona/repo1
           repo1-s3-uri-style: path
           repo1-s3-verify-tls: "n" # Omit or set to "y" for AWS S3 with valid TLS
         repo:
           name: repo1
           s3:
             bucket: <YOUR_BUCKET_HERE>
             endpoint: s3.amazonaws.com
             region: <YOUR_REGION_HERE>
     backups:
       pgbackrest:
         configuration:
           - secret:
               name: percona-pgbackrest-secret
         global:
           # Must be different from the Crunchy repo1-path
           repo1-path: /percona/cluster1/repo1
           repo1-s3-uri-style: path
           repo1-s3-verify-tls: "n"
         repos:
           - name: repo1
           # The storage is shared, use the same settings here 
             s3:
               bucket: <YOUR_BUCKET_HERE>
               endpoint: s3.amazonaws.com
               region: <YOUR_REGION_HERE>
      # The rest of your configuration
   ```

1. Apply the manifest:

   ```
   kubectl apply -f deploy/cr.yaml -n "${NAMESPACE}"
   ```

1. Wait until the cluster reports the `Ready` state:

   ```
   kubectl wait perconapgcluster/cluster1 \
     -n "${NAMESPACE}" \
     --for=jsonpath='{.status.state}'=ready \
     --timeout=600s
   ```

   The Percona Operator deploys the cluster and bootstraps it from the storage referenced in the `dataSource` section.

   The cluster can report `ready` as soon as the primary starts, and then report `initializing` again for a minute or two while the replicas start. The primary accepts connections during this time.

1. Verify that the data was restored successfully:

   - Identify the primary Pod and export it as an environment variable:

     ```
     PERCONA_PRIMARY=$(kubectl get pod -n "${NAMESPACE}" \
     --selector postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster=cluster1,postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/role=primary \
     -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
     ```

   - Verify the data insertion:

     ```
     kubectl exec -n "${NAMESPACE}" "${PERCONA_PRIMARY}" -c database -- bash -c \
      "psql -q -t -d migrationtest -c 'SELECT id, value FROM migration_data ORDER BY id;'"
     ```

     Expected output

     ```
     1 | initial-data-before-migration
     ```

   - Exec into the Pod and check that it is not in recovery state:

     ```
     kubectl -n "${NAMESPACE}" exec "${PERCONA_PRIMARY}" -c database -- \
       psql -t -c "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();"
     ```

     You should see `f`: the instance is read-write.

1. Wait until the new cluster’s `pgBackRest` stanza exists for ongoing backups:

   ```
   kubectl wait perconapgcluster/cluster1 \
     -n "${NAMESPACE}" \
     --for=jsonpath='{.status.pgbackrest.repos[0].stanzaCreated}'=true \
     --timeout=300s
   ```

   Expected output

   ```
   perconapgcluster.pgv2.percona.com/cluster1 condition met
   ```

## Take a post-migration backup

Create a baseline backup on Percona’s own repository path so future restores do not depend on the Crunchy archive.

1. Create the `post-migration-backup.yaml` configuration file. Set `--type=full` in `options`: without it, `pgBackRest` makes an incremental backup on top of the full backup that the Operator takes automatically after the cluster starts.

   post-migration-backup.yaml

   ```
   apiVersion: pgv2.percona.com/v2
   kind: PerconaPGBackup
   metadata:
     name: post-migration-backup
   spec:
     pgCluster: cluster1
     repoName: repo1
     options:
       - --type=full
   ```

1. Apply the configuration to start the backup:

   ```
   kubectl apply -f post-migration-backup.yaml -n "${NAMESPACE}"
   ```

1. Wait for the backup job to complete:

   ```
   kubectl wait perconapgbackup/post-migration-backup \
     -n "${NAMESPACE}" \
   ```
